maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MAYBANK REPORT IN WINNIPEG "FREE PRESS" OF PROCEEDINGS IN HOUSE OF COMMONS
PRIVILEGE-MR. MAYBANK REPORT IN WINNIPEG "FREE PRESS" OF PROCEEDINGS IN HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. My question of privilege arises out of what purports to be a report of the proceedings of this house. I should say that this report does not emanate from the parliamentary press gallery. This report is not an accurate report; it is a complete misreport of supposed proceedings in this house. I do not know whether the error is an error on the part of the newspaper or whether the fault lies with the hon. member who represents Winnipeg North. The facts which I find necessary to lay before the house are as follows:
The Winnipeg Free Press under date of October IS, 1945, has a fairly lengthy report of a meeting of the Winnipeg district trades and labour council.	After reporting on
numerous matters that took place at the council meeting the Free Press publishes the following:
Replies were read from Prime Minister King, Hon. C. D. Howe, L. A. Mutch, M.P.,
S.	Knowles, M.P., Ralph Maybank, M.P., and
Alistair Stewart, regarding the council's resolution passed at a mass meeting in the Playhouse theatre on the question of reconversion, unemployment in the aircraft industry, and the post-war programme prepared by the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada.
The report goes on to indicate the nature of these replies which were received from various hon. members, and then continues:
A letter from Alistair Stewart said that he had brought the matter up in the house but
that Ralph Maybank talked the resolution out, so that no vote could be taken on it. "Afterwards Maybank received the congratulations from government members for his sabotage," said Stewart's letter.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MAYBANK REPORT IN WINNIPEG "FREE PRESS" OF PROCEEDINGS IN HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Order. The hon. gentleman knows that any hon. member may rise to a question of privilege in connection with any matter in respect of which his integrity or honesty are put in doubt, and I would ask the hon. member to state his question of privilege.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MAYBANK REPORT IN WINNIPEG "FREE PRESS" OF PROCEEDINGS IN HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Precisely, Mr. Speaker; that is the point. Moreover, there is also the question of the privileges of the house itself, as you will observe from the remainder of that which I desire to present to you. That which I have read as being the report of a letter by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) is not merely an inaccuracy, nor can it even be called a distorted report of anything that occurred in this house. It might be termed a perversion of the truth, but a better way of describing it would be to say that it is pure fiction and has no relation whatsoever to truth. It is a complete make-up.
The newspaper story states that Alistair Stewart, who is the representative of Winnipeg North in this House of Commons, brought up in this chamber the question of a resolution of the Winnipeg and district trades and labour council which had been passed at a mass meeting, dealing with the question of reconversion, unemployment in the aircraft industry and the post-war programme prepared by the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada. The said Alistair Stewart, the member referred to in the news story, never did bring up this question in this chamber. In fact the said gentleman never initiated anything in this chamber at any time. The said gentleman is reported to have stated that I talked out the resolution which he had brought up and that therefore no vote could be taken on it. That statement, of course, is utterly without foundation. Not content with an excursion into the realm of fancy to the extent already indicated, he goes on to say that government members in this chamber congratulated me for the imaginary sabotage of a mythical proposal.
If the hon. gentleman is correctly reported it is probably incumbent upon us to offer him our congratulations upon his flair for publicity, but at the same time this is a mere fairy tale as far as being a report of the proceeding in this chamber is concerned. I submit therefore that it is not merely my privilege but my duty to bring to the atten-
Veterans Affairs

tion of the house this misreport, which, like all libels, will find its way far abroad as a result of the manner in which it is put out.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MAYBANK REPORT IN WINNIPEG "FREE PRESS" OF PROCEEDINGS IN HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
May I suggest that the
hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Maybank) should know much better than to accept the Free Press as being accurate. What I said in my letter was correct. I am not responsible for what the Free Press says.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MAYBANK REPORT IN WINNIPEG "FREE PRESS" OF PROCEEDINGS IN HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: I said in the beginning that I did not know whose fault it was, but someone is at fault.

speechtext:
The house resumed from Monday, October 22. consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Howe'-Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Trans-Canada Air Lines Act 1937, to increase the capital from five to twenty-five million dollars and to authorize the Canadian National Railways to issue securities to twenty-five million dollars for acquiring the stock of the corporation; to provide authority in the governor in council to create corporations to operate and maintain air services under contract with Trans-Canada Air Lines such corporations to be controlled by Trans-Canada Air Lines; also to make provision for the payment of subsidies to such corporations payable out of moneys to be apporpriated by parliament and with provision for the termination of the present contract for the transport of mails and for a new contract for mail transport.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is not
often I find myself in a position to give warm and wholehearted support to government measures, especially proposals introduced by the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe).

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: I suspect it, right now.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
I hear the suggestion that the legislation is suspect, already, because of my support; but I do rise to express my wholehearted approval of the proposals made yesterday by the minister, so far as they go-In other words, after I have made my favourable comments I shall have something to say about further steps which in my view the minister should take.
My opening comment with reference to the Minister of Reconstruction relates to the fact that, rightly or wrongly, we regard him as a strong devotee of private enterprise. In that field the minister has an enviable record of efficiency and success- I am glad to say he has carried that same record of efficiency and success into such phases of public enterprise
as have come under his jurisdiction. I have no hesitation whatsoever in paying to him a well deserved tribute for the work he has done in organizing Trans-Canada Air Lines, and I also wish to pay tribute to him for the further steps he has proposed from time to time by way of extending the principle of public ownership, in so far as civil aviation is concerned. Yesterday I listened with keen interest to the minister's speech, and I was particularly pleased when at the. close of his remarks he referred to the advantages, in terms of Canadian unity, achieved by the building up of an organization such as Trans-Canada Air Lines. I feel that the more we can think in terms of material improvements having a bearing on other phases of our life as well, the better it will be for us. I suggest that we should not look upon public ventures of this kind only in terms of their material value, but rather in terms of what they do to improve life in Canada in every way.
To refer specifically to the proposals outlined yesterday, may I say that hon. members of this group are whole-heartedly in support of the extension now proposed in connection with Trans-Canada Air Lines services. The . minister indicated that it was the intention to increase the service within the country, both by opening new and more direct routes in some areas, and by adding new aircraft to the routes now in service. Secondly he dealt with new lines to be established for service outside Canada. These he dealt with under the headings of new lines to the United States across the Atlantic, to the West Indies and to the Pacific.
I felt that hon. members in the Progressive Conservative party gasped when they listened to these proposals for the very wide extension of the principle of public ownership, which was so well underlined when the minister pointed out that the extensions would increase five or six times over, the route mileage of Trans-Canada Air Lines.
Hon. members in this group feel that there are certain fields of endeavour which are natural monopolies, and that aviation is one of them. When a field of endeavour is a natural monopoly we take very strongly the position that that monopoly should be in the hands, not of private individuals, but rather in those of the people as a whole. May I repeat our whole-hearted support of the minister's proposal to enlarge the capital set-up of Trans-Canada Air Lines to establish these subsidiary corporations, and to establish government control of these additional services
Trans-Canada Air Lines

Incidentally we are pleased to learn about the opening of services to additional points in the United States, the United Kingdom, the West Indies and in the Pacific area. The really significant thing, however, is that at the outset we are not going to make the mistake of turning this venture over to private enterprise, and then going through all the difficulties involved in trying to get it back at a later time. We are starting out on the right foot, and I congratulate my hon. friend the minister, who is sometimes my en?my, upon the stand he has taken in this instance.
Another reason why I was pleased to note the establishment of the principle of government ownership in our international air operations lies in the none-too-bright picture which presents itself in respect of international civil aviation. I feel deep concern in this matter, and do not wish to say anything which would complicate international relations. But the fact is that the provisional organization we now- have in the field of international civil aviation does not go as far as some of us feel it should go. 'In fact, it does not go as far as the Canadian government sought.
This brings to mind the warm support given by hon. members of this group to the proposal made by the minister on March 17, 1944, for an international air authority. Without reservation I congratulate the minister and the government of Canada upon the part they played at the Chicago civil aviation conference, where they advanced the proposal to which I have just referred. I was pleased with the stand they took, and with their diplomacy in the face of a difficult situation. There could be no denying the fact that by the way they performed at the Chicago conference they helped to strengthen Canada's position in world affairs. If that conference did not develop as some* of us would1 have liked, nevertheless a provisional arrangement was achieved. We are glad to note that the headquarters of that organization is in the city of Montreal, within the boundaries of our own country. In the world of to-day we cannot but be grateful for any step in the right direction, even though that step may be only a beginning.
In terms of civil aviation, the international situation is one which calls for a strong stand and for a definite contribution. I am glad1 to know that Canada's voice in the provisional body which will deal with international civil aviation will be the voice of a government which has already gone on record as favouring an international air authority-with power

and a government that has established its own postion in Canada as favouring government

ownership and control of our own main-line routes, and also our connections with other countries. I hope that in the deliberations that are carried on in connection with the provisional set-up the minister and the government will continue to press as far as they can along the lines of the draft proposal for an international air authority which was presented to us last year.
Lest hon. members on the government side or to my right think that I am simply taking up the time of the committee to pat the government on the back, I shall now say something about the other side of the picture. The minister will have a pretty good idea of what I am going to talk about. It seems to me that the principle of a natural monopoly being best handled by the people as a whole through their government applies not only to our main line routes and our international air connections, but also to the smaller lines, to the feeder routes that play such an important ' part in aviation in Canada.
There still seems to be some uncertainty as to what the government intentions are in this connection. We have had a statement of government policy, and we have had an act which incorporates that policy to the extent that it is proposed1 that within a certain period after the war the railway companies shall divest themselves of the ownership of air lines. I dared to hope when I saw this resolution on the order paper yesterday that it foreshadowed the setting up, not only of crown companies to operate subsidiary lines into other countries, but of crown companies to take over feeder lines in western Canada. I am still hoping that when the bill comes before us its provisions will show that it will be possible to set up a crown corporation capable of operating within Canada lines subsidiary to the main line of the T.C.A. If it is not in the bill, I hope in due course another bill will be brought down to give that authority to subsidiary corporations of the T.C.A.
When the minister made his statement on March 17, 1944, with reference to compelling the railways to divest themselves of the ownership of air lines, he did not go on to the position I am now taking, namely, that the feeder lines should be government-owned. He said that it was the desire of the government to leave that field open to returning airmen who might like to go into that phase of activity. We contended at tKe time, and I think results have borne out our contention, that the chance of a returned airman to break into civil aviation on his own is very slim. We reminded the government of what had

Trans-Canada Air Lines
happened in the early days of bush flying. Those men made all kinds of sacrifices to get civil aviation started, but most of them have since been swallowed up by the larger companies. The larger companies now handle most of the civil commercial flying in this country. This type of flying is now virtually the monopoly of one firm, namely, Canadian Pacific Air Lines.
Yesterday the minister tabled sessional paper 129A, in answer to a series of questions that I placed on the order paper some time ago. One of my questions had to do with the number of aviation firms operating in Canada and what routes they were licensed to fly. The return is much too long for me to read into the record, but I find it divides the companies operating in Canada into four groups. First, there are the companies licensed by the air transport board. These total nine, and they are licensed only for charter service. They do not operate fixed routes; they are merely small taxi-ing air firms. The second group of aviation firms is licensed by the board of transport commissioners. There are about ten or eleven of these Canadian companies operating small feeder lines, of which there is now a great network across this country. The third group of companies is licensed by the Department of Transport, and there is just one Canadian firm under this heading, Maritime Central Airways Limited. The fourth group is a list of United States air transport companies which operate into Canada.
As I say, there is a considerable network of feeder lines in Canada. At the present time the only group of companies operating services of any significance is the group licensed by the board of transport commissioners. I have checked the return and I find that these ten or eleven firms operate a total of sixty-eight routes, of which only eleven are operated by companies other than the Canadian Pacific Air Lines or its subsidiaries. In other words, fifty-seven of the sixty-eight charter routes being operated in Canada at the present time are operated by Canadian Pacific Air Lines or its subsidiaries. The fact that a number of these companies are subsidiaries of Canadian Pacific Air Lines is not obvious from the sessional paper to which I am referring, which simply lists the various companies under their own names. But by making a cross reference to " sessional paper 155, tabed in the house on February 11, 1944, in answer to a question of mine as to what firms in Canada were subsidiaries of Canadian Pacific Air Lines one
finds that Arrow Airways Limited, Canadian Airways Limited, Mackenzie Air Service Limited, Quebec Airways Limited, Starratt Airways and Transportation Limited, Wings Limited, and Yukon Southern Air Transport Limited, are all subsidiaries of Canadian Pacific Airlines Limited. These are the firms, all C.P.A., that operate fifty-seven routes, as I have already indicated. The only three outside of C.PA. that are operating charter routes are M. and C. Aviation Company Limited, Northern Airways Limited and Maritime Central Airways Limited.
The fact that this one firm has such monopolistic control of this important phase of our life makes it obvious that-it is next to impossible for returning airmen or for any so-called small person to get into this field. In order that returning airmen may not waste their lives, their capital and their energy in a cutthroat proposition; in order that we may have the best service for Canada, it seems to me that the course to follow would be to incorporate these feeder lines under a subsidiary company, such as the minister is proposing under the terms of the bill he is about to bring before the house.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Will that give the returned man a chance?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: It will give him more of a chance than he has under the other system. My hon. friends say that they want private enterprise, but here we have a monopolistic firm, Canadian Pacific Air Lines, stepping in and gobbling up the whole show.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: What about the returned men?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: My hon. friend should remember that there is far more opportunity for the returned men under government corporations set up under government control than by trying to get into a field completely held by these private corporations. Canadian Pacific Air Lines did not pioneer in this field at all. The pioneering was done by individual men whose cause the hon. member is now pleading, by the bush pilots who got these small companies organized.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: May I ask a question?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Order. An hon. member is entitled to ask questions only with the permission of the hon. member who has the floor.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
The interjections only underline the point I am making, that these individuals whose cause my hon. friend was
Trans-Canada Air Lines

so anxious to plead tried to do that very thing in the initial stages of civil aviation, but one by one they were swallowed up by the larger corporations. In the early days, C.P.A. were doing no pioneering at all, but later in the. day they came in and bought up ten of the smaller companies who were doing the pioneering and now they have a monopoly in that field.
There are two questions I would like to put to the minister. I should like to know what progress the government is making in implementing its decision that the railway companies must divest themselve^ of the ownership of air lines within one year after the end of the war. I asked that question of the minister a few days ago by placing it on the order paper. My question was this:
Have any steps been taken by the government to form a crown air lines corporation for the operation of feeder air lines in central and western Canada? If so, is the acquisition of the ownership of Canadian Pacific Air Lines by said corporation under consideration?
The answer given by the minister was simply "no". On the other hand when I asked this question:
Has the Canadian Pacific Railway divested itself of the ownership of Canadian Pacific Air Lines? If not, has the government taken any steps designed to achieve this end?
The minister's answer was:
It is proposed to carry out the intent of the declared policy of the government under date of March 17, 1944; namely, to cause the Canadian Pacific Railway to divest itself of the ownership of Canadian Pacific Air Lines within the time specified in the Act to Amend the Aeronautics Act. 8 George VI. chapter 28, effective September 11, 1944. Discussions to this end are under way.
Both of those questions and answers will be found in sessional paper No. 129A, tabled yesterday. I left the latter question until I had given the other, because I liked that answer much better. I am glad that discussions are now under way, and I hope that during this debate the minister will give a report on the progress of discussions to that end.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: To what end.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
To the end of compelling the C.P.R. to divest itself of ownership of C.P.A.
I have another question to ask, because in my view it is not enough just to advocate that the Canadian Pacific Railway company divest itself of ownership of the Canadian Pacific Air Lines. That can be accomplished by the setting up of another holding corporation separate from the C.P.R. taking over the C.PAe. and continuing to operate it as a

private monopoly. This leads to my question: Are any discussions under way with a view to setting up a corporation subsidiary to T.C.A., which might take over these feeder lines and incorporate them into a well worked out rational programme of civil aviation in this country? I feel strongly about these things, and one of the reasons I am taking the time of the committee is that I hope that the government will move in this direction, and there is no time like the beginning of a venture such as aviation to get started off on the right foot. The government has done the right thing in terms of the main line across Canada, and its record with regard to the T.C.A. is exceptionally good; I do not hesitate to give all kinds of credit to the minister and the government for that. I am wholly in support of the proposal now made to maintain as a government monopoly flying from this country to Britain, the United States, the West Indies and across the Pacific. I use the word " monopoly," because if I do not my hon. friends to my right are going to use it in an unfavourable connotation. I am using it in a desirable sense, and I urge that this natural monopoly should not get into private hands, but should remain with the people as a whole through government ownership.
Having gone as far as it has, I hope the government will do two thing: first that it will continue its efforts, and I know it will, to secure the establishment of an international air authority along the lines of the proposal made last year by the minister, and that it will also look into the domestic picture in this country and apply to it the same principle of government ownership of a natural monopoly that it has already applied to the main line routes and to our international connections.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the members of the official opposition are very much interested in this resolution, because it opens up for discussion the air policy of the nation. There are several members of the opposition who wish to ask questions on the resolution in order to get the situation clarified. I myself have several questions to ask. But first I should like to point out to the supporters of the government that those of them who groaned when the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre began his remarks were quite right. They were wise to look at his support of this measure with a good deal of suspicion, because the reason that the C.C.F. are endorsing the government on this resolution is that they aim at socialization of all the means of transport within Canada, not only airways but railways and shipping. They are aiming at the socialization of our whole transportation

Trans-Canada Air Lines
system. They are advocating that already in my own province of British Columbia. That is the reason they speak as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has done to-day. It is all very well for them to talk about helping the small airman to get an air route, but the members of the committee will notice that this was a very secondary consideration; we want to help returning airmen just as much as anybody else; in this case the C.C.F. support is designed to further socialization of transportation in Canada.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
Hear, hear. You are
absolutely right.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: The airmen would not get it under their system.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
I think the minister would be wise to make a statement of government policy on that question. The government might as well decide now whether it is going in the direction of socializing transportation in Canada. So far as the members of the official opposition are concerned we do not believe in it; we do not believe it is in the best interests of the Canadian people.
Also I would ask the minister to give the committee a picture of the domestic air situation at this time. On March 17 of last year he gave a very full review of the domestic air situation. He said there were three types of air lines. First, there were the main lines, which were being flown by Trans-Canada Air Lines. Then there were the feeder lines, being the lines flown north and south, as, for example, from Vancouver into the Yukon, from Edmonton into the Yukon, from Edmonton into the Mackenzie river basin, and down the north shore of the St. Lawrence river. 1 cite those as examples of what were known as feeder lines. The third group were known as the bush or pioneer lines, most of which, I presume, fly on charter or do not have a definitely fixed route. In his remarks last year the minister stated the government policy with regard to those three types of air fines. We would ask him to do that to-day, so that the confusion which has been brought into this debate may be eliminated'.
We think that the committee should be told what lines are to be designated as main lines. It is my understanding that the governor in council has power to say that a line shall be considered a main line, and if that is done the line so designated will be flown by Trans-Canada Air Lines. The minister will correct me if I am wrong. We should like to know what lines not now main lines are to be designated as main lines. We see no reason why that information should not be given to the committee.
We should also like to have the policy on the feeder fines. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has brought them intc the discussion; in fact we should like a full statement with regard to both the feeder lines and the bush lines. We understood last year that the government policy in domestic aviation was that there should be government monopoly of all routes in Canada except small operations. Perhaps the policy did not go that far; at any rate we should like to have it enunciated to-day.
Turning to the question of subsidizing other companies, or making loans to other companies, or buying shares in them-all of which the minister mentioned yesterday-this, of course, is a new departure. No provision is made for it in the Trans-Canada Air Lines Act; it is something entirely new; and we should like the minister to give definite information concerning the companies which it is proposed to buy into or to subsidize. Also we should like to know whether this is to apply only to the international lines, those flying beyond the borders of Canada, or is power to be taken to subsidize and to buy shares in companies concerned wholly with domestic aviation?
Further, we ask the minister to give some details with regard to the three international routes he mentioned yesterday. He referred to the route across the North Atlantic; the route from Canada to the West Indies, which I suppose in due course will be extended to South America; and the route from Canada across the Pacific. We should like to know whether the transpacific route is to be by the north Pacific, that is up through the Yukon and Alaska, or whether it is to be to Australia. It may be that the plan is to fly both routes. Personally I should be very much interested in finding out whether the terminus of that line is to be in British Columbia. There was some talk a few months ago that it might be in San Francisco or one of the other United States cities. Also, whether the route across the north Atlantic to Great Britain is to be flown under a bilateral agreement with Great Britain, just as we have a bilateral agreement with the United States covering the various routes across the American boundary, or whether it is to come under the jurisdiction of the new aviation authority.
There may be other questions arising out of the minister's answers to these questions which I have placed before him.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction) :
speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
In reply to the first question asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, the government policy with regard to the railways and their association with aviation
Trans-Canada Air Lines

was announced in this house at the last session. That policy remains unchanged. Part of the policy was in the form of a time limit. The time limit was one year after the termination of war in Europe, in other words one year after V-E day. That year has not expired. We expect before the year has expired to carry out the policy which was announced in this house. Naturally in advance of determination of the details I should not care to go further at this time; in fact I am unable to do so. I may say that discussions are proceeding as to the best method of divorcing land transportation from air transportation, applied to both the C.N.R. and the C.P.R., and when definite plans have been determined I shall be very glad to advise hon. members of the terms. In the meantime anything I might say on the subject would not be helpful to the discussion.
The other question asked by the same hon. member was, does the government intend to nationalize flying into the north, so-called bush flying? The answer is that the government does not intend to do so. Bush flying was inaugurated as a private service. It is a peculiar type of service. There are whole towns in the north which depend on air for everything they use, for tranporting the persons who visit the town or leave the town, for the supplies which come into the town and for the activities of the town. In addition to that there are much smaller services of equal importance. There is the small mining development where the mining machinery and personnel are brought in by air. Such developments also are served by an air service. Then there is the trapper who goes into his trapline in the autumn, and iepends upon that air line to pick him up n the spring. There is the fisherman in the small lakes who goes in at one season of the year and is dependent upon the air line to move out his catch and to pick up him and his equipment at the end of the season.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Almost daily.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
It is a highly personal service. It was developed by private flyers operating in definite territory. At the beginning of the war those services were consolidated into one large system. In my opinion that consolidation was not helpful to the service, and I should like to see the service returned to private companies.
My belief is that the interests of the north country would be best served if it could be divided into perhaps seven or eight zones and one operator placed in each zone who would be charged with the duty of seeing that the public and the public interests in that zone is served. I believe that if the public interest

in that zone is to be properly served it is the duty of the government to see that that air line can operate at a reasonable profit. The difficulties of the air lines arose in earlier years owing to the fact that unlimited competition was permitted. A private operator might establish a very good service in a zone and begin to make some money, The history was that a second operator moved in and cut the business in two so that neither made a profit. The territory might develop so that they both began to make a little money and a third operator moved in. That was the history of flying in the north prior to the war. All those air lines were taken over by one of the railway companies at the outbreak of the war, because unlimited competition in that area had weakened the financial position of those air lines, with the result that the closing of mines and cutting back of business in that territory made it impossible for them to operate.
In discussing the Canadian Pacific Air Lines let us remember that if the Canadian Pacific Railway company had not adopted the policy of taking over those air lines, many of them would have been bankrupt. I do not know what the position of the government would have been, had any of them ceased to operate. Perhaps the government would have had to come to the rescue. In any event before any decision of the kind was required the Canadian Pacific Railway company bought up the shares of the air lines. C.P.R. has maintained the operation and they have kept the service going into those areas.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: And the personnel.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: The personnel has been kept flying. Anyone who could fly a plane has been busy during the war, either in air line operation or in training schools.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
Senior administrative
officers have all been busy?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Some of them have been busy in this service, but others have had to go to the states because there was no opportunity here.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
It was a pity that all the great political parties take a stand for or against socialization of transportation and industry. I think there is a happy medium and suggest a look into any particular industry before deciding whether it would operate better under private or public ownership. Perhaps I have had as much experience on both sides as has any member of this house. In private practice I used to be the servant of the government and the servant of private

Trans-Canada Air Lines
industry, perhaps in the proportion of one to the government and three to private industry. During the war I suppose I have operated more government industries than any man who ever lived in this country. I think I know the strength and the weaknesses of each type of operation. I can tell hon. members this: there is only one test of the strength and weakness of either private operation or government operation, namely, which can best serve the need of the public of Canada.
In the war years the government could operate many industries and do the job sometimes better than private enterprise. Some may question that, but I believe it to be a true statement. The position changes when the matter of selling the product becomes predominant. During the war the government is the buyer of everything produced by a good many industries, and in those circumstances it can operate industries very efficiently. When it is necessary to sell the product in competition with private industry, in my opinion government operation is entirely out of its field; it is entering a field that private enterprise can handle very much better.
When we look at the air lines I believe that a good portion of the operation of air lines can be better done by the government. I do not think anyone would argue that the post office cannot be better operated by the government than by private enterprise. I think most hon. members would say that the telephone is a natural monopoly. Some would say it can be better operated by the government than by private enterprise; some would say that private enterprise would do it better; but I think we can all agree that it is better operated on a non-competitive basis than otherwise.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: What stand does the government take on it?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: We have government telephones and private telephones. They are both doing well in their field, and we have no desire to change the situation in that regard. In other words, in my opinion it is not important which does it, so long as it is well done.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
What is involved in the word
"better"?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
Better service to the public.
That is the only criterion. After all, it is the customer we have to worry about. It is up to the man who is operating an enterpise to make his place. The person who buys the service is the one who must be served, and the one who can best serve the man who buys the service is the man who should provide it, whether it be government or private industry.
Let us discuss the air lines from that point of view. I should like to discuss them as one neither prejudiced in favour of private enterprise nor prejudiced in favour of public enterprise. I think I can stand in that position on my record, because I have served both and I have been responsible for creating both types of enterprise. We will first consider the mainline services of Trans-Canada. Canada is a country of twelve million people sitting beside a country of a hundred and forty million people. We have to have the same type of service that the country to the south of us enjoys if we are to be equally well served. Our area is just as great as the area of the United States, in fact a bit larger, and we require air service more than does the United States because our population is more scattered. In order to give that efficient service I believe that the main lines should be operated as a monopoly.
At the inception of the project I was not very much worried about who should run the monopoly. My first stand in the House of Commons was that it ought to be run by a group made up of the two railway companies and the government forming a partnership. That did not work out, and it was decided-

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Why?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
-we would place it in the
hands of the government-owned railway. In any event, it was treated as a natural monopoly. It has prospered under that direction. I think we have to-day an air line that is as well operated as any air line in the world. I have been interested, in attending the international discussions, to hear the comment;, about Canada's air lines. I have been interested in the requests we have had from other air lines to send men to serve with Trans-Canada in order to obtain the Trans-Canada technique. We are told that our technique of operating an air line is equal to the best in the world.
It is the intention of the government to maintain the service on the main air routes as a government service. It was started that way. The government made the investment, and the original investment has been added to by earnings accruing from the operation of the system. This service has not cost the taxpayers of this country one cent; in fact the taxpayers have profited financially from the operation. We intend to continue that operation and expand it to meet the needs of the Canadian people' for interurban flying.
Then there is a second class of service, which I have referred to as bush service. I have said already that I believed that was better served by private enterprise. In interurban service we are able to maintain very close control. The air line is paralleled by
Trans-Canada Air Lines

telegraph services, teletype services and a communication service which allow those operating the line to be in touch with every plane in the air for every minute of its flight. A bush service is quite different; it depends upon the operator of the plane,'his knowledge of the territory and his ability to take care of himself in case of sudden emergency. As I say, the bush services were developed by private operators. They know their territory, and in my opinion are better able to serve that territory efficiently than the government would be through operating the service as part of a great enterprise. This type of service calls for individual attention, and I believe if we give an operator enough territory so that he can make a living in that territory and can prosper with its growth, provided that he looks after his customers, that is the ideal service for the north.
Then there is the third type of service in Canada, the charter flights. We are licensing quite a number of charter operations. The charter flyer has no scheduled service and no regular route. He is stationed in a city or other centre prepared to take parties who may charter his plane to any point in or near his territory.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: If I may ask a question there, when a chartered plane sets out from a field does it have to get a permit from some operator to take that trip, say from Fort McMurray to Yellowknife?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: If it is a licensed field the operator is required to check out with the local air authority; the operator of the field is required to make sure that the plane is in condition to fly, but there is no great restriction about it. He must, simply comply with the air rules before his plane leaves a licensed air port.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: What I had in mind was that when one plane is in the air flying north, another plane might be flying south. How do the two planes keep in contact with one another, or how do the fields from which they fly keep in contact with them?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
Before he leaves the field the operator of the plane must file a route plan, and an effort is made through the available services to inform other planes that this plane is in the air flying a certain route on a certain schedule. The charter plane of course is definitely a private operation. A flyer takes out a licence to do charter work; he performs a necessary service, and is restricted from interfering with those who are licensed to operate routes.
I think I have covered all the points down to subsidized flying in Canada. As I say, I believe if we can restore the individual oper-

ator in the north it will be the duty of the government to see that he can live, provided that his work is satisfactory. When the Air Transport Act was passed by this house it contained a provision that the air transport board might recommend to the government subsidies on northern routes payable out of money appropriated by parliament for that purpose. That provision has not been invoked, but it will be used if necessary to establish proper services in the north country. Starting a new route is expensive; business builds up gradually, and if it is necessary to subsidize a new and desirable route in order to get it into operation, the government will use the powers it now has under the Air Transport Act. The subsidy provision of this amendment to the Trans-Canada act refers entirely to foreign services. In starting a line, we will say from Vancouver to Australia and New Zealand-

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Before the minister goes on to the international field, are we to understand from what he has said already that the policy will be to have seven zones with seven different operators flying those zones?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
I could not answer that
question. I have given hon. members my idea of a proper arrangement for the north country. Whether that can or will be worked out I cannot say at this time, but I believe it js the best system for the north as I have observed the operation of air transport in the north country over the past ten years.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
When the minister
was referring to bush sendees I take it he was not describing what the hon. member for Vancouver South calls bush services but to what the hon. member calls feeder lines; is-that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
I think in this country the
two are practically the same.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
That is a distinction I
was going to ask the minister to make.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
Between bush services and
feeder lines? If a bush service flies from Aklavik to Edmonton and delivers passengers to the Trans-Canada service there, it is a feeder service to Trans-Canada and it is also a bush operation. I suppose a feeder service need not necessarily be a bush operation. A bush operation could be described as a service off the main airway. It can also be a feeder service operating on the main airway, picking up the intermediate stops.

Trans-Canada Air Lines

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
You would not call a
line operating from Fort William and Port Arthur to the main line a bush sendee?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Fort William is in the happy position of not being involved in this dispute; it has no such service.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: I am serious about that, for there is a distinction which I believe the minister should clear up. In the minds of some hon. members there is some differentiation between a feeder line and a bush line. "Bush line" would not seem to me to be the term properly applicable, for instance, to that great section of Canada represented by the Minister and his friend from Fort William. I am sure his constituents would not think a line connecting Fort William and Port Arthur with the main Trans-Canada line should be called a bush operation. Perhaps that might be used as an illustration of what we mean and what we think should be cleared up.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: We are answering the question my hon. friend raises by moving the main line of Trans-Canada to go through Fort William and Port Arthur, so they will be a main line stop.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
That is perhaps solving
a number of problems at the same time.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
Might I suggest another
example of a feeder line which could not be considered a bush line. I believe applications have been sent in for a service to some of the gulf islands which lie between Vancouver island and Vancouver, so that business men of Vancouver may spend week ends on those islands. I am sure the gulf islands would not like to be considered bush.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
Well, I would not want to
interfere with the pleasure of those taking such trips, but I would call that a bush line in the ordinary parlance of the trade. All bush lines are feeder lines, but I suppose all feeder lines are not bush lines.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Perhaps you might call ,hem branch lines.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Yes, branch lines.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Does the minister propose o subsidize bush lines or feeder lines? He mentioned subsidizing bush lines. Does he mean bush lines or feeder lines?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
So far I think that the government has not subsidized any lines. My position would be that if a service is needed in an area and cannot be performed without a loss, provided that the operation is efficient I 47696-89
should be prepared to subsidize that service. But if it is not a necessary service, I would not be prepared to subsidize it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
While the minister is making his statement to the effect that the government is not subsidizing lines, would he not also complete the picture' by referring to the amount of money the government has spent in developing routes, beams and meteorological and other services? I have before me a document tabled by the minister in August of last year in which is listed an item for S29 million spent by the Canadian government directly on the development of routes to the north. It also refers to the fact that the Canadian government has agreed to pay to the United States government $76 million for installations of a permanent value. I have had these things in my mind during the discussion which has been going on for the last half hour. Hon. members, particularly those to my right, have spoken as though these private firms flying to the north were doing it entirely on their own. But they have been able to do it only because of the immense amount of help made available to them through government expenditures.
While I am on my feet perhaps I should make a further comment. The minister said that with the folding up of these small air lines, if the Canadian Pacific had not come into the field we should have been denied that service. May I point out that if it had not been for the expenditure of public money on developing these routes, even the Canadian Pacific would not have been able to carry on the service. I am only suggesting that the-minister should complete the pioture. In fact I was going to ask him if he could give the committee the up-to-date figures as to what it has cost the government to develop these northern lines.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
May I point out to the hon. member that all the airports which have been built in the north during the last five years have been built for war purposes. For the defence of Canada and the United States it was necessary to have a chain of airports extending from Edmonton to Alaska. Large expenditures were made on that route, and tremendous quantities of freight were shipped over it to serve the war in the east and1 to assist Russia in her war effort in Europe. Those are matters quite separate from the discussion here to-day.
May I tell the hon. member that the services of which he speaks were in operation before those expenditures were made. While the aircraft use facilities of that type for present day service, I doubt very much if airports have added to the earning power of

Trans-Canada Air Lines

those planes, through the fact that they now operate on wheels where formerly they operated on floats. The expenditures in the north for war purposes are scarcely pertinent to this discussion. However, I feel I should finish my statement, and then let someone else have the floor.
The reference to subsidizing the flying of transocean aircraft, to which reference was made in my statement concerning the amendments, refers to the pioneering of new services outside Canada. So far as the Canada-United Kingdom service goes, may I say that that service has already been pioneered. I believe it can be a profitable service, right from the start. In fact we hope to inaugurate a fare paying service before the end of this year. In the meantime we have practically covered .the cost of the line through the very heavy movement of mail handled, as a result of our troops being in England and on the continent. I think we'need not worry about subsidizing the Canada-United Kingdom service. Nevertheless when we pioneer from Canada south, through the West Indies and into South America, that will be an expensive operation, and in its initial stages it must be subsidized either by Trans-Canada Air Lines, if its funds permit, or, if not, by a government appropriation. The same is true of the Pacific. That is a very thin traffic route, extending some six thousand or seven thousand miles, and it is scarcely conceivable that in its initial stages it can operate without a subsidy.
But I can say this, that the three routes I have mentioned are routes which we believe will ultimately represent a profitable operation. And I can also add that Canada is in " the air in a practical way, and that we do not intend to operate indefinitely any route which will not pay its operating costs. That has been our policy in the past. We have abandoned certain routes because we became convinced that they were not profitable, and our policy in international aviation will be the same as it has been in domestic aviation in that respect.
Mention was made of selling shares of certain companies, or of subsidizing certain operations.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Buying shares.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
Buying or selling, yes. That arose from the fact that several South American countries have a proviso in their laws to the effeet that any air lines operating into their territory must be owned, in certain proportions, by the nationals of those countries. For instance, the law in Brazil requires that any service operating into that country must be owned to the extent of forty per cent by

residents of Brazil, and must carry a certain proportion of pilots who are nationals of that country.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
Will the minister
permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Just let me finish my statement. The purpose is to give Trans-Oanada Air Lines the same freedom in the development of civilian services that any privately owmed competitor would have in carrying out the same operation. I believe I have covered the questions asked by my hon. friend.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
Would the minister say
something further about the transpacific route?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: The proposal is to operate in cooperation with a partnership made up of the government of Australia, the government of New Zealand and British Overseas Airways. The combination of these three will form one company, and Trans-Canada Air Lines will be their partner in the operation. The intention is that the Australian-New Zealand-British Overseas Airways group will operate one flight, and that Trans-Oanada will operate the second flight.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Right through?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
