maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
The minister has made a
statement about this matter, first in connection with the domestic side and then, second, in connection with the international side. I raised some questions about this last year on March 28, at a time that was vital in the history of our empire. One international branch of this matter deals with the Pacific; another has reference to the north Atlantic and the third deals with lines operating to the West Indies and South America. I raised certain questions last year and the year before because I felt that Canada was away behind the times, that if we did not change our policy we would soon be in a precarious position.
I would call the attention of the committee to to-day's order paper. Item No. 6 is in connection with the carrying out of the provisions of an interim agreement which was signed in Chicago. The next matter of business to which I would direct attention was dealt with a week ago to-day when a motion to appoint a committee was agreed to. A year ago when the minister made what I considered was a leap in the dark in connection with this whole matter I proposed that it should be sent to the committee on railways and shipping in order that all sides of the matter might be considered. We should know now what the policy of this country is going to be in view of the rapid progress that has been made in civil aviation.
I wish also to call attention to the resolution that was placed on the order paper on October 47696-891
22, the matter which is now before the Chair. Why is it necessary for Canada to take part in all these secret conferences when parliament is in session? The Prime Minister is in the old country at the present time and he is supposed to be dealing with matters relating to the defence of the empire, civil aviation, trade, migration and other matters of interest to the empire. Why is it necessary to have all these secret arrangements that have been made? As I said last year on March 28, continuing again on March 31:
Why did Canada not seek first a conference with the other dominions in order to formulate an empire policy as a unit? What was the need for all this secrecy in regard to a public matter such as this which is of the utmost importance to the future of the world and the future of our empire? Why were all these star chamber proposals made, when we had the minister and his staff in London at a time when there were also in that city representatives of nearly all the countries of the world trying to devise some definite plan for the progress of civil aviation and the progress of the world in general.
Mr. Curtin and Mr. Fraser appealed to Canada to formulate a policy for the Pacific. Those two prime ministers pointed out that the United States had grabbed all the air routes in the Pacific. In this connection I would refer to the report of the British shipping board. The Americans have a tremendous hold over the Pacific, and they did not get it by accident but by enterprise at a time when Canada was asleep. They have made great concessions to travellers. The United States air service over the Pacific is free, every military pr civilian traveller having the benefit of that route at no cost to himself.
The prime ministers of Australia and New Zealand had a conference on January 17 of last year at which they agreed on a plan for the Pacific. They made an appeal for an empire air policy. Canada has ignored it all and has done nothing about it. As I said last year, Canada now announces an international air policy as though she were a first-class power. The United States will have nothing to do with internationalism; neither will Russia. Russia has made an agreement good for ten years-with whom? With Great Britain. The United States have made several agreements, as I pointed out the other night. These are with whom? They are with the Latin republics in South America and with other countries.
We have had in the C.N.R. some most unfortunate experiences with branch lines, American subsidies and merchant marine. We want to link this up with Canadian National Railways. The Canadian National Railways is public ownership in some ways, but not in others. What is the railway system going to do? The time has come when that system needs more rolling stock for passengers and
Trans-Canada Air Lines

freight. A great need at the present time is more housing, but yet you are going to create some more civil aviation subsidiaries for our railway system, a system which was supposed to be bankrupt a few years ago. That railway system has done splendid work, and I have referred before to the wonderful work done during this war by the employees of the system. We have had an unfortunate experience with the subsidiaries of the Canadian National in the United States. They have received most of the benefits in equipment and rolling stock during the war, before the war and between the two wars. We have had a most unfortunate experience with our merchant marine. Ships that cost a million and a half were sold for $15,000 to $30,000. We have had a most unfortunate experience with the useless duplication and waste in the branch lines of the Canadian National system across Canada. We have had reports by royal commissions on these things, but we have ignored all of their recommendations to avoid errors in transportation.
I have the report of the British shipping board. The British merchant marine has been on the seas for over two hundred years. Under their policy they allowed ships of all nations to enter their harbours under user, but retained sovereignty over them, and I suggest that the same principle should be applied in the matter of civil aviation.
We have a British navigation policy, under which any ship can enter our harbours and land its cargo. They cannot enter our coastwise trade on the Atlantic or Pacific, but they can land their goods at our ports. That policy has proven in navigation a success for two hundred years, and has made Great Britain the great ocean-going country she is. The same principle should be applied to civil aviation, which should be free the world over, with user given, but not sovereignty.
The old country, with New Zealand and Australia, appealed to Canada to act as a link in an all-red empire air route, but in January and March 1944 we rejected that appeal. We should never forget what the other privately-owned railway company, the CJP.R., has done to build up this country, by the building of the air branch lines and the development of ocean traffic, as well as what it has done in~civil aviation. I repeat that government monopoly of transportation in the air will not be a success if we now branch out into an international world effort over the head of the mother country, and other dominions.
I say further that we need a constitutional change. Why should one minister of the crown be able to walk all over the world and

make agreements respecting the Pacific, the Atlantic and South America and any place else over the head of parliament in session, or political pledges given to foreign countries? What kind of constitution is that? A pledge which in time will take the form of a treaty, no doubt. It could not be done in the old country, and I would recommend a change in our constitution so that the minister would first have to report to the cabinet.
Is this the time to embark on a separatist scheme like this over the head of the other dominions? I say no. I say further that no individual politician, and we are all politicians, should obligate the government of this country in any matter which has not first been submitted to parliament. We have seen what happened in military matters by not following that policy, and we have seen what happened at Locarno, for instance. We have seen how some agreements made over the head of parliament have led to a second war. The first duty of yes-men in Germany was to find out what the dictator wanted and then to do that very thing. Are we going to be a lot of yes-men? If so the authority of parliament is gone. Yes-men are not all astrologers. Perhaps if they were, we would be better off. Germany, Italy and Japan all depended on yes-men to keep their authoritarian governments in office. Are we going to be yes-men? Are we going to act aver the heads of the other dominions to pass this separatist agreement? If so, we are headed for disaster. As I said, there should be a constitutional change. No minister of the crown should be able to act over the head of parliament. It cannot be done in the old country.
I asked the minister the other day a question about the interim agreement made at Chicago. I asked if the report had been tabled and he said that he did not know. I do not know whether it has been tabled since or not, but we are to be tied by this resolution to everything that was done at Chicago.
There is another side of this picture. We have an international defence board. As I said before, it is all board and no defence. It seems that the minister has ignored that board altogether when laying down his policy. We have also to consider the Atlantic. Has Britain ever been consulted for cooperation in such a policy as this? During the war Britain made an agreement with the United States by which it got fifty-six of her old destroyers and in return she gave the United States a ninety-nine year lease of her naval bases, practically freehold, from Newfoundland right down to British Guiana, and according to the congressional debates the United States is not

Trans-Canada Air Lines
going to give up those bases. We had better stay in the pond before we wander out into the lake. Internationalism is all right, but it presages a perfect world which we never will have. We must never forget that Canada is a country of only eleven million people. None of the dominions are able to go it alone, and if we and the other nations of the commonwealth do not hang together we shall hang separately.
We need not think that we are a first-class power in the Pacific. The mother country was in such straits in the war with Germany that she had to leave the Pacific to the United States, and I do not criticize that at all. But one of the mistakes Canada made during all this war has been that we have surrendered to Washington. too much political, military, financial, and economic initiative. The people of the, United States, our great ally, would respect us much more if we told them what our views are not only in regard to this question but in regard to other questions.
The most important feature of all, the defence feature for the future, the minister has apparently not considered at all. Let me read a few paragraphs'from Sir Edward Grigg's book on "The British Commonwealth" which has been recently published. He says:
Until the present century it was only naval power that this island had to fear; but the advent of the aeroplane has established a new menace which commits it still more deeply to a vital interest in European affairs.
The role (which used to be hers) of semidetachment combined with a vital interest in certain aspects of European affairs now passes to Canada. She must suffer the reluctance to be involved which Britain has always herself felt and shown; with this from her own experience Britain can fully sympathize. But facts will compel the Atlantic democracies as they have always compelled her. An accumulation of potentially hostile naval and air-power upon the western seaboard of Europe and northern Africa would menace Canada and the United States, not merely with destruction of their sea communications and trade, but With attack upon their peoples at home; and they are furthermore exposed to a danger which has not troubled Britain for at least a century past-namely, that if their foreign relations were unwisely handled or their defensive preparations in arrear, they might be threatened -with simultaneous war upon their Atlantic and Pacific coasts.
He goes on to say:
So far as the United States are concerned, the issue rests with the American people; but their decision, whatever form it takes, cannot affect the need for the closest possible understanding between Britain and Canada. The latter's position is of vital importance for the development of air communications, and this should be planned in concert by the British and Candian governments. It is also of consequence that British and'Canadian measures for the welfare of sea transport and the protection
of sea communications should be complementary. Canada is now too great a country to be regarded as a British or American or Anglo-American protectorate. Her resources are vast; and if her population increases suitably and proportionately, she may well be the equal of any but the greatest powers before the end of the present century. It is of moment to the whole commomvealth that British institutions should prove their strength in her. the greatest oi the younger nations of the British family. She is the first example of what nationhood within that wide brotherhood can achieve as it passes from semi-dependence to the full stature of national maturity; and the destines of the empire now lie as much within her lands as in those of the British people.
These are wise, true words. At this time we should have plain speaking and clear thinking on this question.
I contended last year that there should be a chair of aviation in every large university in Canada. One of the hopes we had last year when this matter was under discussion was, that, next to agriculture, aviation would prove to be one of the main sources of employment for the boys returning from the front. But if we have this kind of international policy our place will be taken by competitors whose resources and experience exceed our own. The minister has spoken of the planes which have been selected. I predict that they will be obsolete by the time that the extensions,' which will require a year or two years, are carried out. Nor do I favour the policy of handing over empire bases for international purposes; they should not be retained subject to user by other countries. Where would we have been in this war had we surrendered all those bases to international control? Where will we be in the next war if their ownership passes into other hands?
The policy which the government is adopting over the head of parliament will not, I predict, be a success. I was about to refer to this the other day in connection with the motion for the setting up of the committee on railways and shipping. We are adding today to our obligations in connection with this department, and more subsidiaries to be, and I can say this, that the Canadian public, with the experience of the vast expenditures on the C.N.R. in the branch line days of Sir Henry Thornton, are long-suffering, but there is a limit to their patience regarding this particular problem, and in my opinion the limit has been reached. Thoughtful men are concerned at the number of government subsidiaries and outside boards that are spending money like water. There seems no hope of parliament regaining control.
I suggest to the administration that one of the most important things to be done is completely to reorganize Trans-Canada Air
Trans-Canada Air Lines

Lines. Look over the board of directors. Millions upon millions of dollars are to be expended. Has our finance minister, whom I am glad to see back with us to-day, been' consulted about this? If you had the responsibility for a private railway or a steamship company, would you entrust that great public ownership venture to Mr. Symington and Mr. Henry and the other gentlemen, some of whom were mentioned a few years ago in this house in connection with a light and power scheme, the Beauharnois of blessed memory? These are the men who are to head this whole world extended system, branching out all over the world into the Pacific and Atlantic oceans and international transportation generally, over the head of the mother country, and the other dominions, without any consideration of the effects on all allred empire air scheme of this policy. I do not doubt that they are good men, I have nothing against them personally; they are splendid citizens, but they have too much to do now in -other lines, and no time for this as another venture. If we are to have a publicly owned monopolistic system, at least give it a chance with public ownership men. I repeat that I believe the whole Trans-Canada Air Lines should be reorganized. In this connection it is of the utmost importance that we have an agreement and an understanding with our great ally the United States and with the mother country. What has been done in this direction? We have not heard one word about the results of the empire conference in London in January, 1944, when Canada was represented and did not aid in it. At the present time the Prime Minister is over there: we do not know what he may have done regarding this matter.
I have recently expressed myself on the policy of adopting this big programme and going extensively into this business over the heads of the other dominions: Hansard, March 31, 1944, page 2046:
Reference has been made to the selection of the Douglas DC-4 by the Trans-Canada Air Lines. It is obsolete. They say that the Lancaster is unsuited for civilian purposes, but it has been shown by Handley Page and others in the old land that some of the bombers can be readily adapted in a few days for use as transports, and also Lancasters by simple changes in design by research at Malton.
I do not believe that in connection with this aviation problem we have given sufficient attention either in this war or the last to scientific' research. ... I believe that the government will waste a lot of money by utilizing the Douglas DC-4 for its civilian air service. A much better plan could be worked out along the lines I have indicated. Canada should try to take the lead in the field of design and should prepare a definite policy for the next twenty-five years. Fundamental changes will occur in the future. Aviation in Canada is yet only in
IMr. Church.]
its infancy. Research, design and experimentation will be more important than ever. In Canada and in the empire we are on the threshold of a grand new age which will revolutionize aeroplane construction and the development of aeroplane engines. In this field high speed is essential to supremacy. Problems of all sorts arise; science and research will provide even lighter alloys and nerv types of wings, engines and parts which will withstand various climatic conditions the world over.
I do not think Canada should have a monopoly in connection with civil aviation, any more than she should have a monopoly in connection with design. No doubt immediately after the war improved aircraft for the transportation of passengers, emergency foods and many other articles will be absolutely necessary, because when the war is over the railways and, other forms of transportation will be choked. So it will be of the utmost importance that there be close cooperation and mutual understanding between Great Britain, the United States and the dominions.
I believe this question, instead of being a secret with the minister and the government, should be considered by the committee on railways and shipping, which dealt with one aspect of this question the other day. It should hear all sides of the question. Trans-Canada. Ait-Lines, Canadian Pacific Air Lines and private lines in this country, which carried on the work of civil aviation between the two wars, should be heard and a proper policy should be adopted. We are now embarking upon a policy of complete isolation from the mother country; we are going over the heads of Australia and New Zealand, and I say we are at the parting of the ways. I warn hon. members of the danger; I say we should stop, look and listen to the advice of those who have seriously considered this matter. When the young people come back from the war and look for employment, where will they find it?
For these reasons I oppose the international feature of this project. I am in favour of a red all-around-the-empire scheme. Indeed it is necessary to have such a programme to solve our own problems and to enable the mother country to recover. She is suffering as hardly any other nation has done; unless we stand behind her in this aviation programme she will simply revert to being a small island and become a second-class power like Denmark, and the British empire will pass into liquidation. The time has come for clear thinking and wise and plain speaking on these empire matters in this house.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
Those of us who live in
western Ontario or in northern Ontario are intensely interested in Trans-Canada Air Lines, Of course we know that T.C.A. is a baby of the minister, and it is not surprising to know he is extremely proud of his boy-because there is nothing feminine about the T.C-A. After this baby has been half starved during the war we find that the minister wakes up this House of Commons and the country to the fact that this baby must be fed. He

Trans-Canada Air Lines
realizes, as a wise father would realize, that there are two sources from which this baby can get the food it needs. One is the House of Commons and the other is the natural resources of the northland. He is calling for support from both. We at the head of the lakes-and that includes the two progressive cities of Fort William and Port Arthur-believe that the minister is wise in calling for additional expenditures to feed this lusty baby, and I am sure that he will get it.
He then initiates those feeder lines. We have thousands of young airmen who risked their lives over Germany. They have initiative left; they do not want to be tied down too much. They have been accustomed to running their own show in the air pretty well, and now many of them are beginning to organize feeder lines all over Canada. I hope that the minister will continue to give them the encouragement they need and thus feed the lusty baby from -those feeder lines.
I should like to say that before the war I was in room 16 with the minister and three specialists who wanted to get an order for a plane or planes to serve on the T.C.A. The minister said, "What is the name of your plane?" Well, of course, it was not known; it had never been tried out. I can see the minister with his smile set, striking from the shoulder. He said, "No plane will be tested out on the Trans-Canada Air Lines." You can imagine me just sitting back and saying, "thanks", to the Great Aviator that we have a man like that at the helm so that no young man's life will be risked.
We at the head of the lakes are very much interested in the Trans-Canada Air Lines. We have had pictures of Fort William, Port Arthur and the Thunder Bay district, of course, feeding it on the Trans-Canada Air Lines. We have been told that we would be on the direct route, and that is natural. The minister himself sees that that is the natural route for the Trans-Canada Air Lines. Look at the distributing point. Fort William and Port Arthur are the very centre of Canada, the breadbasket of the world, as I said the other day. Why should not we be on the main route of the Trans-Canada Air Lines? I speak as the mouthpiece of the Thunder Bay district and say to the minister: "Success to you; look after your baby; feed him well. Feed him well from the feeder lines all over Canada and you will have an air parent that will live long after you have closed your eyes in sleep."

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
I am going to ask only a few questions, because to make a speech on this matter at the moment seems to me to
be entirely out of place. We can do that on the second reading of the bill. However, I should like to get a little clarification on a matter over which I am concerned. Yesterday I asked the minister a question on the orders of the day. My question arose from a rumour that appeared in La Presse of Montreal to the effect that negotiations were under iway to expropriate the Canadian Pacific Air Lines. The minister replied to my question as follows:
The government has not given consideration to expropriating the shares of Canadian Pacific Air Lines, and is not doing so at present.
In a return tabled in reply to a question asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, some information is given, and I would gather that negotiations must be under way because of a quotation which appeared in this morning's Gazette. The quotation is as follows:
Mr. Howe said discussions were under way with a view to carrying out the announced government policy of compelling the Canadian Pacific Railway to divest itself of ownership of the Canadian Pacific Air Lines.
These two replies do not jibe, and I should like further explanation, because, as the minister said to-day, it is the announced policy of the government to compel the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to divorce itself from the operation of airlines.
The minister outlined the policy of the government in a speech he made on March 17, 1944. In that speech he was not a bit friendly toward the good work which the Canadian Pacific had done. I am not here to defend the Canadian Pacific Railway any more than I would get up and speak in defence of any other company that had done good work. I myself am not interested in any company, but I am interested in defending any company that does a good job.
I had determined to make a trip to inquire into air service over the far north country, and I received a good deal for joy from it. I had to go by the Canadian Pacific Air Lines because there was no other way for me to go. I presume this line from Edmonton to Fort McMurray, from Fort McMurray to Fort Smith, and from Fort Smith to Yellowknife is what the minister would call a feeder line. The same thing applies if one goes the other way, from Fort Smith to Fort Resolution, from Fort Resolution to Fort Providence, from Fort Providence to Fort Norman and from Fort Norman to Norman Wells. I found the service excellent. I made up my mind that when I had an opportunity I would suggest to the minister that the airfields could be improved. The airfields on the eastern route are just the ordinary gravei runway airfields and there is a great deal of
Trans-Canada Air Lines

traffic over them. I do not know whether or not it is a paying traffic, but there is a lot of traffic over that route. The airfields should be improved with the object of opening up the country more rapidly. When I was there I do not believe there was an 'airfield at Yellowknife. My trip on the last occasion did not take nie over to Yellowknife. When I went to Yellowknife I went in a pontoon plane that rose and alighted on the water, but I am told there is a wheel plane field now at Yellowknife.
I ask the minister to consider in his programme having plane fields much farther north. I met quite a number of prospectors representing very large companies that are up in the Coppermine area. Of course they had to go into that country by pontoon planes. All of them suggested the advisability of having somewhere up in the Coppermine area a field that wheel planes can alight on, because once the frost comes down there is no way of getting out of that country, since the pontoon planes cannot alight on ice until it has formed in sufficient strength to support them.
I suggest to the minister that a field to accommodate wheel planes be constructed at Aklavik. There is quite an area there on which a field could be constructed. I made it my business to make a thorough examination both north and south of Aklavik, and Doctor Livingstone, the government representative at that point, pointed out a very good position which on examination looked to me to be all right too. There is quite a community there, and as it is the outpost of this country on the Arctic I would imagine that it would be good business to construct a field in that area on which wheel planes could land. I want a further explanation from the minister as to what he means by feeder lines in relation to the position of C.P.A. in that country, and I only mention C.P.A. because ;hey have no other feeder lines there. I do lot know why Trans-Canada has not decided to go into that country unless, as the minister has suggested, it is because the department would not allow a line to be started that could not be operated at a profit. Somebody has to* operate these lines which do not make profits. I do not suppose C.P.A. makes any profit, and all the more credit to it for opening up that country. I found them very satisfactory and the airfields on the west line from Edmonton to Whitehorse are 100 per cent. They are the best I have seen anywhere; large, well-lighted and with fine buildings.
In his speech yesterday the minister spoke of starting a line to fly from Whitehorse to
rMr. MacNicol.]
Fairbanks. Is the same line going to carry traffic from Edmonton to Whitehorse? If so, it washes out C.P.A. as far as that route is concerned; if not, then that line will be away off by itself. I feel that in the course of his remarks the minister at least should have paid a compliment to that great railway which operates those air lines in that far north country at its own expense. The Canadian Pacific has been a pioneer railway, and I often contemplate the great men who built it; Mount Stephen, Van Horne, Beatty, and the other great men who pioneered throughout the west and I presume did more than any equal number of individuals to open up that whole country for the benefit of Canada. They are worthy of a bit of praise, but not one word was said by the minister on behalf of the C.P.R. or the C.P.A. I am not here to defend them. They need no defence on my part. They are quite able to take care of themselves, but the C.P.R. and the C.P.A. do deserve some praise in this house for what they have done. Now they are again pioneering in that country in the matter of air transportation, and personally I am not in favour of wiping them out. I believe in supporting the T.C.A. to the limit, but I am a believer in competition, and I can speak very highly of the service I got from C.P.A.
Perhaps I might tell the committee one instance the like of which I do not think could be found anywhere else. When the plane I was on arrived at Fort Good Hope everyone got out to see the little old church built by the fathers who were in that country many years ago. It is quite an ornate structure and I took many pictures. Soon I exhausted the film in my camera and went back to the plane to get more. To my surprise I did not see my suitcase anywhere, so I asked the pilot if he would mind getting into the plane and handing me my suitcase, because I wanted a film. The pilot got in and turned over all the suitcases but could not find mine. When he came out he said, "I guess I must have left it on the dock at Norman Wells." I said, "Well, you might as well have left me there. There is no use in my going to Aklavik and all through that country unless I have my camera and films." So he said, "Just wait [DOT] a minute." Then he hopped in the plane and went back over a hundred miles to Norman Wells to get my suitcase which had been left on the dock. That is service.

speechtext:
If the T.C.A. was operating that line and would not do as much for its passengers I would not call it a very good service. It was not my fault the suitcase was left on the dock; I had paid a handsome sum for that ride, which I enjoyed very much.
I should like to ask the minister, too, if consideration has been given to the establishment of airfields in the Arctic. As the minister knows, United States lines are planning to fly over our far northern country. Since it is only 7,700 miles from New York to Chungking flying over northern Canada over the west end of Baffin Land, that is likely to be one of the routes, and I should like to know if this legislation contemplates the construction of airfields in our far north so that it may become the main line from the great American cities to the Great Asiatic and European cities. I should like to know further whether the proposal mentioned by the minister yesterday, or the record tabled yesterday by the minister in reply to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in reference to the taking over of C J.A. means that this really is to be done. I can tell the minister that I heard much condemnation of that proposal in the north country. I went there to ascertain what the feeling was. Everywhere I stopped, at Fort McMurray, Fort Smith, Fort Resolution. Fort Norman, Norman Wells, right down to the Arctic ocean and also at Dawson and Whitehorse in the Yukon, as soon as the plane stopped I got off and asked everyone what they thought about C.P.A. service. 1 can tell the minister I found 100 per cent approval of that service and general regret that there was a possibility of its being wiped out. So many said, "Well, if C.P.A. is wiped out and we have no competition we will just get what everybody gets where there is no competition, and that is not very good service."
I was glad to hear the minister say it is not the intention to wipe out what are called the-bush planes. I found prospectors in the far north greatly worried over the possibility of the bush service being wiped out. I asked one man why he was worried, and he replied that the big planes, that is C.P.A. or T.C.A., have to fly on beams, and I think there is only one beam in the whole north country, at Norman Wells, although there may be one at Whitehorse. He also said that the big planes would stay on the ground perhaps for two or three days, until they got the order to go. Of 47696-90
course you could not blame them for that. I had to wait for two days at Fort McMurray before going north on the C.P.A. plane, but a judge who went north with me to Fort McMurray got on a bush plane at Fort McMurray. I inquired about that, having in mind what I had been told, and I was informed that the bush planes will follow the rivers and fly if it is at all possible. They will follow the Athabaska river and the Slave river; then they will cross Great Slave lake to Yellowknife; and if they are going further north they will go on to the Coppermine river, and so on. They keep right down where they can see the water, and since they are all float planes they can come down on the water if that becomes necessary. So that I am glad to hear there is no intention whatever of wiping out that service.
Let me just conclude with this. I am going to suggest to the minister that when he speaks again he be big enough, and I know he is, and fair enough, as I believe he is if he thinks of ' it at all, to give some credit to that great pioneer railway and its aviation service, both of which have done so much for this country. The. minister ought not to confine his remarks to what has been described as his baby. Trans-Canada Air Lines is a pretty big baby and, anyway, the minister ought to be big enough to have a couple of babies.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT

Divesting orders have been
made many times. It is only four or five years ago that a divesting order of exactly the same kind was issued in the United States. United States which it had to dispose of. My financial friend must have heard of orders of that kind in connection with investments, about which he knows a great deal. If my hon. friend would think more deeply he would know what a divesting order is.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT

As for air lines in the north, we are gradually building airfields to serve important settlements. We are building airfields where there are communities. For example, we are building airfields at Yellowknife, where a large mining operation is in progress, an operation which will require twelve months service. We are proposing to build an airfield at Red Lake, which is also a mining centre largely dependent upon aircraft. We are planning to build landing strips at other points in the north.
My hon. friend suggests an airfield at Aklavik. Aircraft which operate into Aklavik must serve other points which must be served by hydroplanes. If we had an airfield at Aklavik no aircraft could travel to it on wheels.
I would expect my hon. friend would get the best of service. I should think that any air lines which gave any other kind of service to Mr. John R. MacNicol, M.P., world traveller, would not only cease to prosper but would not expect to survive. I am rather shocked, though, that they forgot his baggage. It seems to me that he did not get the service to which his experience and standing in the community would entitle him. Perhaps I have answered the questions.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: I do not wish to go into this matter on a national or on a provincial basis. I am concerned about my own constituency.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Perhaps it is as big as some countries.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Yes, perhaps it is. The minister will know that Canadian Pacific Air Lines hold the franchise to Norway House. While they hold the franchise, they do not give a service. Bush pilots who are willing to give that service are deprived from doing so.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: By whom?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
That is what I want to know. It is impossible to have any communication with Grand Rapids and Norway House. If one sends a wire to have a plane come in, he has to pay for every seat on the plane

Trans-Canada Air Lines
both coming in and going out. This would be an extortionate figure for the ordinary man or woman to pay.
However, the other fellow-I do not know whether you would call him a bush pilot- is willing to give this service. He may come under the chartered plane service to which the minister refers. Under the new policy which has been discussed this afternoon will such chartered planes be permitted to come in to pick up a sick person, for instance, or a doctor, and bring him back? When one has to pay for every seat on a plane the cost is prohibitive, and people, are left to die. Someone may say that we never had this service before. My answer is that we are living in a modern world, and that the people in my constituency want the same service that is given in other parts of the country.
Hon. members to my right give credit to Canadian Pacific Air Lines. I would give the credit to my buddies of the last war who pioneered these routes, thus making it possible for Canadian Pacific Air Lines to buy them up and make more money out of them.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
I should like to ask two or three questions, the replies to which will be of interest to my constituency. Yesterday the minister said:
Trans-Canada Air Lines will establish additional services from Halifax to Boston, from Toronto to Cleveland, from Toronto to Chicago, from the lake head to Duluth, from Victoria to Seattle and from Whitehorse to Fairbanks.
Is that to be the end of that flight? It is a short flight and from a financial point of view would not be very attractive. Is that flight from Whitehorse to Fairbanks to be extended further south or further north?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: The policy of the government is to operate all international routes under Trans-Canada. Obviously the physical operation of the route from Whitehorse to Fairbanks by Trans-Canada is impossible, so that a sensible arrangement has been made. The licence has been issued in the name of Trans-Canada, with Trans-Canada subleasing the operation to Canadian Pacific Air Lines.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Does the minister intend to supplant Canadian Pacific Air Lines with Trans-Canada Air Lines on the flight from Vancouver to Whitehorse and from Edmonton to Whitehorse, which is a daily flight? Canadian Pacific Air Lines now operate a semi-weekly flight between Whitehorse and Dawson and certain mining camps. Will those flights be taken over by Trans-Canada?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
No consideration has been
given to Trans-Canada entering into those operations.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: I can assure hon. members that services no\y in existence will be continued. There is a lot of nonsense being talked here, if I may suggest it. Everyone knows what a change of ownership means. It does not mean that you close down the service.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: What is the real purpose behind this bill? Is it being introduced merely for business and commercial reasons or are there questions of high politics and high policy involved?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: I suggest it' is a little of both. The requirements for air transportation in Canada have expanded greatly and are at present not being met by Trans-Canada Air Lines. The purpose is to increase the capital of Trans-Canada Air Lines so that sufficient equipment can be provided to develop fully transport within Canada. It is also the policy of Canada to establish certain transoceanic routes. Whether we are doing it for prestige or for profit, the fact is we are doing it in the national interest. We are doing it for the same reason that a country establishes a shipping route or any other kind of route outside the country. For whatever reasons, we have decided to do it and the purpose of this bill is to provide the funds to enable us to do it.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: We have always relied on private enterprise to pioneer routes of all kinds, such as our railways and shipping. Why should there be a departure with regard to air?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: I cannot see why there should be. The interurban routes of Canada were pioneered by public enterprise. Because we have a capable public enterprise, that public enterprise seems to the government to be in the best position to pioneer the transatlantic route. Therefore we are going to use that instrument for that purpose.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
Whatever our views may be about private or public enterprise, we all would like to have an understanding of the facts. I should like the minister to explain one statement he made. As I understood him, he said that T.C.A. has never cost the taxpayers one cent. I should like to have him explain that a little further. I would call the minister's attention to what he said yesterday. He referred to the fact that the statute
Trans-Canada Air Lines

originally provided that the payment by the post office for the carriage of mail in Canada should be on a sliding scale calculated annually on the basis of the revenue and costs of operations of Trans-Canada Air Lines during the preceding year.
I observe that in furtherance of that policy, from 1943 to 1944 the revenue from the carriage of the mail rose from S3,o15,000 to $3,800,000, an increase of some $500,000. That revenue was needed because there appeared to be a surplus of only S7,000 with that additional revenue. The minister explained later on in his remarks that a change was being made because more flexible provisions were required in connection with the payments for the carriage of air mail.
Would the minister be good enough to tell us whether there are any incidental services which are provided for Trans-Canada Air Lines and which are not paid for. I take it that there are radar and weather services and what not, as well as emergency landing fields that are provided. I would ask the minister to explain that statement. We should be able to understand exactly whether all costs, direct and indirect, of operating T.C.A. are in fact borne by T.C.A. I say this quite seriously. Those who believe in public ownership should be more anxious than anyone else to have the true picture, because we do not want to fool ourselves about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
The committee on railways
and shipping examined the officers of the air line on the very question my hon. friend /has raised here. A great deal is said about mail payments, but let me remind my hon. friend that anyone who wishes to send anything by air must pay a premium for that service. For example, at the present time if my hon. friend wishes to send an airmail letter he puts a seven cent stamp on it- That seven cents is made up of one cent war tax, three cents for first-class mail and three cents for a surtax for airmail. I regard the three cent surtax for airmail as just payment by the post office for the service rendered by T.C.A.
This question undoubtedly will be discussed in the committee. My information is that the payments made by the post office for the carriage of air mail by T.C.A. do not exceed the surtax on the letters. I should like to make that clear because it is often referred to' as a subsidy. As a matter of fact it is paid for as a service. It was provided that the rate of payment by the post office would decrease as the earnings of the line increased. As a matter of fact the post office originally paid sixty cents a mile. Last year I think it
iMr. Macdonnell.l
paid about forty-one or forty-two cents a mile. If the present arrangement had been continued, the rate would be lowered still more for next year.
The reason the change is being made is that the carriage of mail is no longer the principal business of Trans-Canada Air Lines. It is an important business, but there is a great demand for air accommodation in excess of the needs of the post office. The result is that when it became necessary/ to put on four, five or 'six schedules a day the post office said, "we need only two or three schedules; we object to carrying the whole line." By mutual agreement it has been decided to drop the automatic reduction feature of the mail rate and work out an arrangement perhaps on a ton mile basis.
When my hon. friend speaks of landing fields and radio beams he must remember that these were used by others than Trans-Canada Air Lines. The R.C.A.F. could not have operated in this country without the radio beams that also served Trans-Canada. In fact, perhaps two-thirds of the radio beams in the country were built during the war to serve war purposes. Just as shipping has its harbours and lighthouses, the air service has its airports and radio beams provided as government services. Certain fees are paid for using them, but they are not enough to carry the service, although we hope that in time they will.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
I was interested in a remark made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre a little while ago in connection with the C.P.R. and CJP.A. To my way of thinking he made that remark because he thinks it is popular among the people generally, but instead of condemning the C.P.R. on the ground of its being private enterprise I think he should take into consideration what it has done in building up this country. It is all very well for people to make political capital out of remarks of that kind, but everybody knows that the C.P.R. has done much to build up this country, and the country can get a little too much of the kind of talk my hon. friend indulged in.
The hon. member said something else that I did not like, and the Minister of Reconstruction also said something a little like it. He said that this party would be aghast at the thought of public ownership, but I would point out that the Conservative party was the first party in Canada to bring into being public ownership when it instituted the great hydro electric system in Ontario, which has been remarkably successful. There is a place for public ownership and there is a place for

Trans-Canada Air Lines
private ownership. We in this'party do not want to be controlled body and soul by seme individual at Ottawa. As my hon. friend the member for Davenport has said, the C.P.R. at one time was almost synonymous with Canada. It has built up this whole country. Of course it has made mistakes, and so has the C.N.R. and the C.P.A.; there is no question about that.
The one thing that concerns me more than anything else in connection wtih this bill and government policy is this: Are we to get under the government's policy the service that I think this country requires? At the present time we are not getting that service. How long will it take us to get it? We have a good transcontinental service serving the large cities like Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver and Victoria, but there are many cities in Ontario that do not get a service, such as Hamilton, Niagara Falls, Fort Erie, Owen Sound, Sault Ste. Marie, Moosonee, Temagami and all that tourist playground in the north. The government's policy is to wait until someone else provides the service and then take it over. But who will form a company to provide a kind of circuit service in the province of Ontario to serve all these different towns I have mentioned that are now without a service? I think we need such a service, with jumps of from seventy-five to one hundred miles. That would serve various towns in Ontario that are now without service. But who are you going to get to do it unless some guarantee is given that the company that starts it will be able to carry on and not have the business it has developed taken away from it by being absorbed into Trans-Canada Air Lines?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Will my hon. friend tell me what line we have taken away from anyone or propose to take away?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: You propose to take away the C.P.A. lines after they have developed a great service.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: I said that we did not intend to take them over.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: But the precedent is there. What kind of guarantee are you going to give these people?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Is it intended to keep on the airfield at Gander, Newfoundland, as a base for ocean air traffic? ,

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
That is a difficult question to answer at the moment. We would like to continue it, but we are subject to an agreement between the United Kingdom, Newfoundland and Canada so far as the use of
this field for civil aviation is concerned. There will be conversations within the next month to determine this question, but at the moment I cannot answer my hon. friend's question positively.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Will Goose bay come into the conversations?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: It is in the same position. These airfields are in Newfoundland and are subject to the laws of Newfoundland. We have not worked out an agreement required to determine the future use of these bases. Gander does not belong to Canada but is being operated by Canada during the war years.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: But the T.C.A. are now using Gander?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Yes, we operate a service there. The field itself is not operated by T.C.A., but by the R.C.A.F. We have a small building there to handle passengers, and that is all. We operate there, just as we operate into three other airports in Newfoundland.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: I suggest that if you put in equipment there it would certainly be more comfortable for the passengers who have to stay overnight and sometimes for three or four days. I have another question. The air'force operates a meteorological service through the north country. Does T:C.A. pay for any of that work?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: No; the meteorological service antedates flying. It is a service for all Canada, which we have had for many years. It forecasts the weather for farmers and gives weather forecasts for the cities, and we have used the service for flying purposes. But the meteorological service is a service for all our citizens.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Who owns the Gander airport?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
It was built by the United Kingdom at their expense. The ownership was later transferred to the government of Newfoundland. Goose airport was built and paid for by Canada, on lend-lease from the government of Newfoundland for ninety-nine years. It is the property of Canada but, being located in another country, it is subject to the laws of that country, in so far as its use for civil aviation is concerned. We are in the position that we own it, but if the government of Newfoundland says that we cannot use it, we cannot use it.
Trans-Canada Air Lines

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
There is a very important point involved here which we are losing sight of. Regardless of whether these transportation services are privately or publicly owned they are primarily designed to give service to the Canadian people. I think we shall all agree that in the past we have been extremely wasteful in the construction of railway lines. Windthorst, the town where I live, is serviced by the C.P.R., and two miles north is the Kipling-Regina or Brandon-Regina line of the C.N.R. These lines run parallel two miles apart, sometimes widening to a space of three or four 'miles. Then there is a strip of territory to the south where people have to travel more than twenty miles to get to town, a great area wherein there are no railways, buses or air lines. I believe that so long as you have competing private firms servicing transportation in this country you will have that sort of thing. The constituency of Qu'Appelle, which I represent, has a very good train service, and there are also two buses travelling in each direction every day alongside of the main line of the C.P.R. So that the people have four choices every day, two buses and two fast trains, while there are great stretches of territory where nobody has any transportation at all. I believe the only way for the country to have a rational kind of transportation is to have it socially owned, and plan to cover this country to serve the needs of the Canadian people.
When we say that only the C.P.R. gives service, that is a terminological inexactitude; it is not correct. Last year I came to Ottawa three times, and I have come here twice since the session opened. Sometimes I go by Canadian National and sometimes by Canadian Pacific, depending on who has a reservation for sale. The service is equally good. The line of the Canadian National is not quite so rough, and a little shorter. That is the only difference. We can allow our prejudices to blind us to the thing we are trying to do, but if it is transportation in which we are interested let us plan to cover this country with transportation instead of allowing competing lines to run along the same tracks and leave other large areas without service.

If hon. gentlemen opposite wish to carry this amendment it is quite all right with me, because the time is very short. We have only one hour. Perhaps this is the last hour we shall have to discuss this bill. May I continue with my argument in favour of this change? I might state that under the old grain exchange methods seventy to seventy-five per cent of the grain grown was sold during the first three or four months of the crop year, which would begin the 1st of August. In the following three or four months many farmers sold a very large percentage of their grain simply because they were compelled to do so owing to existing conditions. Some of this grain was bought in by legitimate channels. Much of it was bought by speculators and held for higher prices. The effect of this was that a large number of farmers., having in many cases grown large crops, had those large crops used as a penalty against them. By this I mean that while they had the expense of planting and harvesting those crops, the marketing conditions that obtained during the grain exchange time worked against them. The futures system provides protection for banks, elevator companies and millers. In my opinion the interests of the farmers were not protected, and that is one of the things with which we as members of parliament should be concerned.
Again, the grain exchange does not find markets for any of our grain. It is a place where buyers do business, but as far as finding markets is concerned no such business is performed-by the exchange. One of the greatest objections we have to the exchange is that it cannot operate without speculators. In case anyone should question this statement I am going to read from the report of the Turgeon commission of 1938. At page 183 of that report the commissioner had this to say:
I have mentioned the "imperfections" of the futures trading system, and I know that in the eyes of many, the greatest of these is its dependence upon the speculator. And the fact must be faced that this dependence, while not absolute, is substantial not only in Winnipeg but in Liverpool, as the evidence shows. It has well been said that there are only three classes of buyers in the wheat market: (1) those who have immediate need of the wheat, (2) hedgers who buy to insure their transactions,

and (3) speculators who buy and hold in the hope of making profits but also at the risk of making losses. When buyers of this last class are absent, or are present only in small numbers, the market becomes weak and prices fall. This was the situation. which existed in 1931, when the government was urged to send somebody into the market to take the speculator's, place, and the situation was met by the' institution of stabilization measures.
I said at the outset that I was opposed to the grain exchange and that in making this statement I felt I was voicing the opinion of many farmers in western Canada, including organized agriculture. The organized pools of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba presented briefs to the grain inquiry commission, and I quote from those briefs as they are referred to at page 39 of the report. This is the opinion of the three pools:
We are satisfied that the futures market does cause fluctuations not justified by the supply and demand for wheat, and this fluctuating price does not necessarily reflect world value. Indeed, it would appear to be true to say that the futures market is not a system of intelligent merchandising; it is merely an example of irresponsible mob blundering. This tendency toward instability in price, which many farmers are convinced is aggravated by speculation, is one of the most serious indictments numerous farmers level against the futures market.
Since I have been farming in Canada, for the last number of years, I have seen the price of grain fluctuate close to thirty cents a bushel in a day, without any apparent change in the quantity of grain available, and I think it will be readily recognized that farmers who had sold or delivered wheat, who had stored wheat and taken a certain advance on it, were closed out when that fluctuation was downward. This meant that somebody else took possession of the wheat, someone who was in there for the definite purpose of gambling. We may be told to-night, and I expect we shall, that farmers have gained an advantage of quite a number of cents a bushel because of the operations of the exchange. I do not know where anyone can get figures to prove that statement. On the contrary, I would say that if it had been stated that farmers lost a number of cents a bushel through the operation of the grain exchange, that would be much closer to the truth.
According to the last report I have, in 1942 there were 109 brokers, eighty-five of whom were dealing in futures and twenty-four in cash wheat. Under the grain exchange system we find that millions of bushels of wheat which do not exist are traded, and that this trading brings to the brokers a commission on every sale made, regardless of the fact that the wheat does not exist and that it is merely a paper transaction. Of course these trades

Wheat Board Act
* are detrimental to the farmers. At the present time on the Winnipeg grain exchange-and I believe the same is true of the Liverpool exchange-brokers are being paid large amounts of money for which they render no service whatever. A certain commission is paid on all grain sold or bought, and those commissions are distributed among the brokers as an organization. In my opinion that should not be permitted. These men should be given an opportunity to get out and do something worth while for a living.
In the past the wheat board has served and is still serving a useful purpose, and in my view we should do everything possible to see that all our grain is handled by that board; To-day wheat is a national problem, and we -and by that I mean all Canadians-cannot afford to have it handled by the grain exchange. This affects Canada as a whole, not only the farmers. It is realized that a large percentage of our wheat is exported and that we cannot carry on successfully while wheat , and other grains are traded and sold on the exchange. In my opinion the wheat board should set up its own selling organization. In that way it would save the farmers of this country quite a little money and at the same time keep in operation the programme which is in effect at the present time, with the government taking over the handling of all our grain.
I think lion, members will realize that under present conditions we must have purchasing power in the hands of the people if we are to carry on successfully. We are told that a depression is coming. One of the best ways to avoid a depression is to keep purchasing power in the hands of all our people. The greatest potential market in Canada for industrial goods, as in the world at large, is to be found in rural areas. Some thirty-three per cent of our population are engaged in farming. These farmers represent the one undeveloped reservoir of demand for manufactured products. These people are short of everything from farm tractors to kitchen stoves, hats, shoes, paint and nails. If their purchasing power can be maintained the greatest industrial expansion of the twentieth century can be initiated. If the farm people are impoverished and farm prices are low, industry loses its market and labour loses jobs. These are facts which every Canadian knows and appreciates.
In my opinion, to-night we should depart from that practice which has been adopted since private members' days have been restored to us this session, of talking out bills.
Let us discuss this matter intelligently, without going all through the woods; let us give this matter the consideration it deserves, and let us decide it here to-night.

That is the general nature of my reasons for being against this bill.
The hon. member for Battle River has suggested that to keep the grain exchange closed would be a help to the farmers. While he did not speak at great length, he did not give any indication as to the manner in which he thought they would foe helped. There is nothing in the past to indicate that the closing of the grain exchange would be an aid to the farmers. When the government of Sir Robert Borden closed the exchange, it certainly did not do so with the intention of helping the farmers, nor have I ever heard any suggestion that it was closed for that purpose.

Wheat Board Act
As a matter of fact during the last war the exchange was closed on a rising market. Any person who has observed the graph line showing the price trend of that time would see that prices rose steadily, and when they reached a certain high point the grain exchange was closed. Surely, just looking at those signs, one would not say that the action was taken to help the farmers, nor is there any probability whatsoever that it did in fact help them at that time.
I am not criticizing the legislation of that day; I have no doubt that the over-all picture of the war at the 'time made it necessary. I fancy the truth of the matter is that prices under the open market system had become so high that Great Britain could not continue to pay, if those prices were allowed to continue ro increase.
I remember hearing Mr. Motherwell, when he was in the house, asserting very often that by closing the grain exchange at that time the farmers lost a great deal of money, and he used to have some impressive figures to support his view. I do not 'believe it is necessary lo give statistics, because opinion on the point must foe speculative in large part anyway. However, it would not appear that at that time the grain exchange was closed for the purpose of helping the farmers, nor would it appear that its closing had such an effect.
So far as the closing of the grain exchange a few years ago is concerned, the case is the same. The grain exchange certainly was not closed at that time to help the farmers. The grain exchange being closed a few years ago, if we take that act just by itself, did not help the farmers. I do not think any person who had anything to do with the closing of the grain exchange-with effecting its close- would say, in the first place, that he was motivated by a desire to help the farmers by that act or, second, that he ever believed it would have that effect.
The grain exchange was closed at that time on a rising market. I do not remember the date when wheat was seventy cents a bushel, but hon. members will remember that at a certain time that was its price, Hon. members will remember ,also that the price rose a cent or two, then a little more, and finally it got up to a fairly high price. My recollection is that the price went along fairly slowly from seventy cents to about ninety-five cents, but that after it passed ninety-five cents it rose more quickly. It is said that the wheat board was casting many bushels on the market to stem the upward rise in prices. I do not know whether that is the fact, but that was freely asserted and the picture in those days certainly did look that way.

I suppose we shall all come out all right in the end, no matter what happens. The hon. member says that certain organizations assert that they would like to see the grain exchange remain closed. He has never given aty reasons, nor have they, to show how they are to be benefited. As a matter of fact, the grain exchange does not have to be used by anybody. As the name "exchange" implies, it is not anything more than a convenience. The wheat pools did use it, and I think the Scottish cooperatives have always used it, but they did not have to. I would imagine that at times the wheat pools and the Scottish cooperatives did not use it; at times they did and at times they did not.
As a matter of fact all these exchanges were created in the past because merchants met together at some place to do business together. Eventually an organization developed. Of course that is well known; that would not be controverted by anyone. All these exchanges developed in about that way. The fact that a convenience is held open to its members does not obligate any person to use it. Grain exchanges do not raise the price of wheat; they do not lower the price of wheat. They reflect only what the price of wheat is. It is conceivable that the operators on the exchange can lower the price, and it is conceivable that the operators can raise the pfice; that must be admitted and that brings one to say this: There never can be any objection to regulating any organization in case there be abuses.
But it is an entirely different matter to say that men may not establish a convenience for the purpose of trading as long as no person is
Wheat Board Act

compelled to use it. In other words, there is nothing inherently wrong in trading in grain or any other commodity, either on an exchange that may be formed for the purpose of convenience or in any other way. It might be objectionable if farmers, or other individuals wanting to make a sale, had to use the grain exchange because there was no other agency, but such is not the case. There is the wheat board ready to take grain from everybody at whatever the contract price happens to be.
There can be two means open. There can be the grain exchange, the ordinary channel, and there can be the other method whereby the board itself would take the product from the farmer. This policy was in force for a long time. The two of them ran side by side. I do not profess to know all about the matter, but it would seem to me that that might be a good way to continue for a time; that the one could be alongside the other for the future. Very often we find that a combination of methods of that sort is good as a means of balance and checking of one policy against another policy.
I have said that I believe that the approach being developed toward the closing of an organization of this sort is. bad because it introduces more .boards of the .same sort. It will be only a matter of time before we have a board for every commodity in the country, numerous boards set up with the aim of destroying the profit motive, which in my opinion is not anything like the objectionable devil that those who would exorcise it claim it to be.
The bill does not actually say that the grain exchange should be kept closed for ever and a day, but the hon. member has admitted that it is in that direction that he aims, that it was substantially for that reason that he asks the support of this house for his measure. I think we are in agreement there. The bill really aims at the removal of some of the restraints upon the wheat board while it imposes certain other restraints upon the board. For example, at the present time the wheat board is under instructions to act in all respects according to declared government policy. The wheat board is subject to the continuing direction of the government by order in council. The bill would cut that down to a certain extent and leave the board wider discretions than it has at the present time. Surely that is a move in the wrong direction. If the government is to take responsibility, for policies, surely it ought to have the right to dictate those policies. Surely the hon. gentleman would not desire to have a board with untrammeled powers, with unlimited discretion. If that sort of thing is done it will be not merely inviting irresponsibility but actually putting

a premium upon it. It seems to me that if the government is to stand with the money of the people of Canada behind any proposition, it must keep control at all times and be responsible for that money. That is not to say that the policy of the government in these respects cannot be criticized just as it can be now, but if you have it that all the policymaking is left in the hands of a board with practically untrammeled discretion, then you have no means of influencing policy at all.
The sponsor of the bill also complains about payments that are made in the way of brokerage fees. I believe that the brokerage fees they have been paying arose by reason of the quick closing of the exchange. There is something to be said on behalf of . the brokers Whether the hon. member thinks they lead a useful life or not, the fact of the matter is that agents of one kind and another have not been able over the past several hundreds of years to receive fees without doing some service for them. Organizations such as were operating on the grain exchange were not paying, over all the years in which they traded in grain, small brokerage fees to brokers and getting nothing in return. It is not the nature of man to do that sort of thing.
May I say this with reference to brokers and agents generally, and referring to the suggestion that brokers do nothing for their money? I know we do not need to employ a real estate agent when we want to sell a house, but when we do not employ an agent we have to put' ourselves to some inconvenience ; perhaps we have to wait longer to effect a sale, and a number of other features very often make it desirable to go ahead and employ an agent. We feel we get a value. A value, too, is obtained from grain brokers or brokers of any commodity, it does not matter whether it is grain or anything else. If you take away the business of brokering some person will have to be brought in for the purposes of doing their work, and in the long run there will probably be no saving whatever to anybody. At any rate, when it was decided to pay a number of brokers in connection with this work, it came about in this way. The grain exchange was closed without warning. That was the first step. These brokers had a vested interest in their business. Many of them had paid a great deal of money for the seats on the grain exchange, which immediately became worthless. It was in these circumstances that the grain board decided that there was work which some of these men could do. The board continued to employ them to carry out cash grain sales. The cash grain brokers are the

Wheat Board Act
only ones, of course, who have been employed by the grain board. All the others who are called futures brokers were not so employed, but the cash grain brokers were.
There is one feature which is worth while considering in connection with this sort of thing. If a government suddenly takes away the means of livelihood of anybody it is no more than fair that sympathetic consideration should be given to him, not to the point of keeping him in idleness or anything of that sort, but to see whether there is not some useful purpose he may serve.
