I realize that my time is very short, but I am willing to risk the tribute which was paid to the speaker who has just concluded his remarks.
When I look at this bill I cannot but feel that it involves consideration of one of the great factors in our whole economy, namely the grain market. It is not long since when we were willing to accept, as a tribute to the productiveness of our great country, the fact that we were the bread-basket of the world. Indeed, we produce in the agricultural sphere a volume of products which compares favourably with that of any other part of the world.
I had a very great friend, the late Hon, James Malcolm, who at one time was the dominion minister of trade and commerce. If I refer to some of the thoughts he conveyed to me, I wish it understood that I do not seek in any sense to quote him, because it would not be fair for me to do so at this time. But I remember one thought he left with me, that the moment you seek to defeat the law of supply and demand you are indeed rowing upstream; you are pulling a heavy oar. Therefore I say that when you seek to interfere with these natural laws you invite the risks which are run by those who try to regulate in an artificial way one of the great principles of human existence and human activity.
As I think back over the days that have passed I recall an experience we had- following the first great war, indeed as late as the early thirties when it was generally considered that the millers of the world required Cana-

dian wheat for mixing purposes, and we decided that they could not get along without our own natural product, Canadian No. 1 hard wheat. But one of our largest purchasers, the British buyer, was not satisfied to pay the price we then demanded, and turned to Argentina. I am led to believe that up to that time Argentina was a grazing country, but with the British purchasers seeking to buy its wheat Argentina realized that it had a market for another product, and much of its grazing land was turned to wheat production. Rather than help ourselves we created another competitor. So I say that we should approach very carefully anything which would have the effect of regulating the -marketing of wheat. I come from an agricultural constituency, and I am indeed much concerned about the prices which our farmers may receive for their basic products. But I have been told by members of the grain trade, men -who -are willing to risk iheir financial future on their success in this enterprise-and I myself, sir, am not a technician in any sense of the word-that a grain exchange is necessary to the-ir success, that as they purchase they sell against futures; and if I accept that as reasonably correct-and I have no reason to doubt it-I must concede that the grain exchange is a necessary part of our economy. Therefore may I suggest that we approach with much caution anything which has to do with the arbitrary regulation of the price of grain.
I realize, sir, that the time has arrived when I should say to you that I cannot conclude the re-marks I had intended to make, and remind you that the hour is nine o'clock.

I am sure we are not going to exchange punches all evening, because I am a short-winded fellow.
There is in this bill something fundamental with which I think I should deal more particularly. This afternoon I was pleased to hear* the hon. member for Davenport and the hon. member for St. Paul's make reference to the Canadian Pacific Railway company. As one from a rural constituency who has never experienced the set-backs and heart-aches of the stock market hon. members will understand that I have no brief for any transportation system, but as a student of history I believe I can say the Canadian Pacific Railway company has played a prominent part in the development of this great nation. They have indeed pioneered, and I do not like to hear their names slurred or slighted. Because, after all, while some may say they reaped a great reward, believe me, in the early days the capital entrusted to their care was venture capital, and no one knew what the reward might be. In the sense of the great national unity which to-day we profess to admire, they played their part in binding this great nation with bonds of steel into one great unit. It is our responsibility to develop that unit.
Therefore I say that the Canadian Pacific Air Lines is, likewise, a pioneer in the air field. We have it from the Minister of Reconstruction himself, that had they not taken over those lines which were in danger of going into receivership, there would have been no service there to-day. So that, as one who believes in the rights of people, I subscribe to the theory
Trans-Canada Air Lines

that the future transport development of Canada must take into consideration railroads and governments combined.
Certainly we have lost nothing by having the Canadian Pacific railway as a competitor with the publicly-owned Canadian National railways system. I am sure I shall not be misunderstood if, as a traveller and as one who has enjoyed the services of both systems, I make the statement that in my experience I have not found any service to equal that of the Canadian Pacific Railway company. I do not say that in any unkindly spirit, because there are no people on earth more hospitable than the personnel employed by the Canadian National system. My experience has been that they have gone out of their way to look after the comfort of passengers. But the nearer one gets to a monopoly, the more difficult it becomes to make a comparison.
The Minister of Reconstruction said yesterday afternoon that we have established one of the greatest air lines in the world, and I am proud of that fact. May I say to hon. members to my left that all of us have a big stake in the future transportation problems of Canada. I have no reason to object to provision being made for the development of Trans-Canada Air Lines. They have rendered a service, and I wish to be perfectly fair to that ^organization.
I am not a private ownership man, in the sense that I am opposed to public ownership; nor, conversely am I a public ownership man opposed to private ownership. But I do believe, sir, in the theory of efficiency. At present I happen to be charged with the responsibility connected with the chairmanship of the public utilities board in my home city of Owen Sound. We are faced with a problem which I believe private enterprise or private ownership would solve. It is not an easy problem; rather it is a difficult one. I find myself at odds to know how to deal with it.
While the Minister of Reconstruction has admitted that Canadiin Pacific Air Lines assumed the responsibility for certain transportation facilities in the dominion, I do not believe those air lines have ever paid one cent of dividend. As a matter of fact I believe they have shown a deficit, a fact which I suggest indicates a desire to risk capital in the possible future development of the air lines for which they have accepted responsibility.
This brings me to the important point first discussed by the hon. member for Rose-dale (Mr. Jackman). Unless we are prepared to give the green light to private enterprise, we cannot expect venture capital to take a chance in the future development of our

country. I say that to hon. members of the C.C.F. and, particularly to the hon. member for Qu'Ap.pelle (Mrs. Strum), who spoke this afternoon about a Canadian Pacific line running to a certain station in an almost parallel line with the Canadian National. Does the hon. member think for one moment that the Canadian Pacific Railway company, or any other private enterprise, would dare to develop the line she suggested was so necessary, if it did not feel there was some security in that development?
I offer this to hon. members as food for thought. The fact remains that unless we have some organization through which we can make comparisons, it is difficult to determine the efficiency and economy of the operation. I believe that is a fair axiom.
When estimates have been under discussion in the house I have heard my leader and other hon. members ask for comparative estimates, and for information as to the amounts spent last year or the year before. A mass of figures means very little to the average person. Therefore I repeat that the nearer one gets to monopoly, the more difficult it becomes to make a comparison as to efficiency or economy of operation.
There is another factor which I suggest has been overlooked. I know that in Owen Sound public utilities such as hydro, water works and gas pay no taxes. I wonder how much the Canadian Pacific Railway company, which admittedly is the largest taxpayer in Canada, and which has risked its capital in saving air lines which otherwise would have gone by the board, has paid in taxes to the treasuries of the respective municipalities in which it operates, and to the dominion treasury. By the same token, if we are to compare efficiency in operation, I think it is only fair to ask if Trans-Canada Air Lines pay taxes to the municipalities in which they operate, and how much the dominion treasury receives in taxes from that organization. I might ask the same question in connection with the Canadian National Railways, were they up for discussion this evening.
During the days we are inclined to describe as the hungry thirties, when our transportation systems were showing huge deficits running into upwards of hundreds of millions of dollars, the Canadian Pacific Railway company, the largest individual taxpayer in Canada, was required to pay its share of the deficit on the business of its chief competitor. So that I do not hesitate to rise as a champion of individual ownership, while at the same time being prepared-

C.P.R.

Trans-Canada Air Lines

speechtext:
I do not care whether the minister has the records or not.
The hon. member for Davenport paid a great tribute to Canadian Pacific Air Lines; and, as one who has been vitally interested in the development of the north country and the remote areas of this country, I say that the minister is doing a disservice to those areas when he tries to put that great air transportation system out of business, because it was not until Canadian Pacific Air Lines came into being that those who were connected with the mining industry in remote areas felt a certain amount of security in their transportation problems.
The minister must know that not an air transportation system, other than Trans-Canada Air Lines, when you take them from the auditors' point of view, shows a profit; there is not a bush transportation system which has made money in Canada. If there is one, I shall be very glad if the minister will contradict me and give me the name of the company. When we can get a company like Canadian Pacific Air Lines to give us good service and take the loss we are indeed lucky. I think the minister must agree with me that C.P.A. are- supplying a service to the remote areas which is very necessary. Nobody in the house has a greater knowledge of air transportation, to remote areas than the minister himself unless it be the hon. member for Rainy River; they both come from areas where there has been great activity in mining because of air transportation, and it seems to me that the minister should think ofthose districts which are so closely connected wuth his own riding, when he tries to force out of business a company which has given and is giving good service. I suggest to the minister, the hon. member for Rainy River and any other hon. member who is interested in the question of air travel that they go into the mining areas and find out, from the people actually living there, -what the conditions are in districts which can be reached only by plane, and for several months in the year cannot be reached at all; let them ask these people, whether or not they are dissatisfied with the services which the Canadian Pacific Air Lines supplied to them.
It seems to me that if this 'bill is passed, and if all the things which the minister desires come to pass, we shall have a dictator of air control in this country, and that will be the minister or his successor. Whatever happens in the future, nobody will be able to go into the air transport business without the permission of the Minister of Transport or the minister for air, or whoever he will be in days to come. I think we should consider definitely
whether we should vote money for this bill because on a straight dollars and cents basis we will not get a return for the money we put up.
What I should like to ask the members of this committee and the people of Canada is, are we prepared at this stage to enter again into a system of transportation that will bring about deficits of many millions of dollars a year in the years to come? It is true that the Canadian National Railways are possibly paying their way, but the heyday of'war will soon be over and we shall go back to the day. of deficits of a million dollars a week. If we give the minister the power that he is asking for I can foresee the day when we shall have deficits on Trans^Canada Air Lines of a like amount. I think a great deal of consideration must be given to the whole business of return on the capital to be put into it.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
There are one or two matters I should like to clear up and suggest to the committee before the question is put. This afternoon there was much talk about the bush pilots and the small operators servicing the mining industry, particularly the small and isolated mines, the prospecting industry and the prospect mines. I have said this before in this house, but apparently I have to say it again. The reason why the small operators went out of business was that the prospecting industry was reduced to such a low level by the taxes imposed upon the mining companies that there was no incentive for the prospector, the young mining company or venture capital to go into these new territories, in the outlying parts of what we now like to consider older Canada, and develop them before the war.
I speak of northern Quebec and northern Ontario because it is an amazing thing that when we thought of the north country we used to think of it as around Noranda, Kirkland Lake, Timmins., Red Lake and so on, that gold-bearing break which runs through that country. But when one thinks of the new area like the Yellowknife, which is nearly fifteen hundred miles farther north than that again, it will be seen what a tremendous job air traffic has 'to do in the development of mining in the future.
This brings me to one more point which I should like to bring to the attention of the committee. I mention this because I am not a member of the special railway committee. I shall not have the opportunity to appear before that committee and ask questions. I am sorry that is so.
The minister has said that we have three types of operation in Canada, namely, the large transcontinental main line, Trans-Canada Air Lines feeder lines and the bus-h operators.
Trans-Canada Air Lines

There is, however, another type of operation, and that is the type of service which is now being furnished by Canadian Pacific Air Lines, which I shall call the major pioneer. This is an operator operating over very great distances, operating services on which it is unlikely to receive any net profit for some years, but on which it hopes, as the area builds up, to receive a very considerable return. It is hoped that the Yellowknife, the Great BeaT area, and all the new territory, and possibly some of the territory farther west than that, will be found to have minerals in such volume as to pay for the opening up of the area. That area probably will not be serviced by surface transportation for some time to come. Probably there will be major fields which will depend almost entirely on aircraft for their very life. Before those communities can be built up to a size that will give a return to the aircraft company, whatever its name, under whatever guise it is, -to make it profitable, it may be a period of years. Therefore I suggest to the committee that the position of a large pioneer, with sufficient financial reserves behind it to be able to stand the gaff for the unprofitable or building years, ought to be taken into consideration ; furthermore, that such operators should be encouraged.
That has been the history of most of our enterprises in Canada. We do not find things easy. As the years ahead are going to be difficult we must look for deficits. I suggest to the minister that if a large company adequately supported with sufficient capital is not operating these air lines we shall find that whoever does operate them will either decrease the services or ask the government for a subsidy.
If the government takes over the air lines serving the Yellowknife, for example, or if the government owns some major north and south air lines what will happen? For years the minister charged with the responsibility of running this air line will have to come into this house and report deficits, and the deficits will be growing. What will happen is this: The minister will be faced with the treasury board. The treasury board will be on his neck all the time saying: "Can you not cut down that service to the Yellowknife? Can you not cut down the deficit here? Look at what we shall have to face in the house when we report those deficits." That is why I suggest to you, sir, that the government should not operate air lines in these pioneer areas. When I speak of "pioneer" I speak of large pioneers; I am not speaking about

bush pilots now. These large pioneer fields must not and should -not be a government function.
I have never been satisfied that, because the United States divested air transport from surface transport, we should automatically do the same thing, or that it is wise. Our conditions are quite different. In the United States there certainly was a. doubt as to whether the railways, if they owned the air lines, would develop them. Only recently I was reading the history of commercial air transport in the United States, and in particular the history of T.W.A., which went through many vicissitudes. In the beginning they found1 it very difficult to get money, and the only way they could get it was by means of a very large mail subsidy. I do not know if the committee will remember the scandal that was disclosed in connection with putting money into these pioneer air lines, and the log-rolling and political skull-duggery, if you like, that went on until, in either the first or second Roosevelt administration, they had to take over the mail contracts entirely and give them to the army. Then it will be remembered that immediately after the contract to deliver mail was given to the army there was a series of serious crashes, with many pilots killed, and the whole system of airmail in the United1 States very nearly broke down.
At one time T.W.A., when it was T.A.T., had a certain amount of capital invested in it ' by the Pennsylvania railroad. Following that, General Motors Corporation put a good deal of capital into it. Then it went through many difficulties, reorganizations and mergers, and after a great deal of violent manoeuvring I believe General Motors .sold out control to Lehman- Brothers, one of the greatest investment trusts in the world, and the Atlas Corporation, another great investment trust. Eventually they in turn sold out to Howard Hughes, who made such a success of T.W.A. in conjunction with the two pioneers, Frye and Richter.
I need not go on, but that has been the history of nearly all air lines in that country. They have been up against it to get money; they have been held as corporations and monopolies, at various times, but eventually they began to pay. It was not until they began to pay and became big business that they began to stand on their, own feet. Our air lines -began to operate in 1937, just when the air lines in the United States were beginning to pay. I should like to give the committee a few simple figures to show exactly what happened. In- the years 1935 to 1938

Trans-Canada Air Lines
there was an average annual increase of nineteen per cent in air miles travelled. In 1939, however, that increase jumped to 42-2 per cent, and in 1940 to 64-2 per cent. In 1935 the major air lines in the United States travelled 314,000,000 passenger miles; in 1940 they stepped it up to 1,145,000,000 passenger miles. There is no question that Trans-Canada Air Lines have done a good job, but I would point out that they came into the air picture just when every line on the north American continent was coming into its period of profitable operation. T.C.A. came into the air picture at the psychologically correct time, and they could not avoid making a success of it. Because they did make a success, all power to them. Because they have established a magnificent record) for safety, all power to them. Because they have done such a good job, I repeat, all power to them.
Before this resolution is reported, I believe the question of making our major pioneer divest itself from the pioneer long distance air lines, simply because it is a surface carrier, should be considered very seriously. I believe that point should be considered also in regard to the Canadian National Railways. Both the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific are transportation systems. I believe fears are bootless that because an air line is owned or controlled by a railway it will not give air service. I believe that because they are both in the transportation business an air line can become a very helpful co-partner of its parent railway. I believe there are places in Canada where an air line and a railway can and should cooperate in the handling of passenger and freight traffic; and I am not yet convinced that because the Americans have divorced the air line from the railway it is advisable for us to do the same thing.
I should now like to say just a word with regard to bush pilots, the men who put Canada on the air map. The bush pilot was responsible for bringing Canada into the lead over all countries in the world in regard to the amount of air freight carried. Our record in connection with air freight, passenger miles and the development of- bush pilots is unique in the world. We cannot, as the minister has suggested, go into the dog-eat-dog, cutthroat competition of the past. I offered the suggestion that in the country north of the main transcontinental airway there should be some sort of zoning. The suggestion was that the zones should be perhaps 300 miles wide east and west and that in each zone a bush company should be licensed and given a virtual monopoly. This would permit adequate 47696-91
air service in that zone, and if a company made a success oh its operations it would be protected from other companies coming in and taking its business away from it or cutting rates. I pass that suggestion on to the committee, because it has received somewhat favourable comment in the aeronautical magazines of this country.
Therefore I should like this committee to consider very seriously whether the government is the proper agency for the operation of transatlantic and transpacific air lines, and, second, whether it is in the best interests of Canada to have the railways divorce themselves entirely from air transport.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
There is one question I should like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Reconstruction. It is in connection with the request made by the hon. member for Vancouver South that the minister provide further information as to the policy of the government in connection with branch and feeder lines.
As I recall it-and I submit this with deference-the minister did not give a satisfactory answer. He made some reference to bush lines; in fact he almost had us bushed, because he went on to say that he did not know the difference between feeder and bush lines, and left the matter there. I think he should bring us in from the bush, and make a definite statement of policy, or give some consideration to the matter and make his statement later.
I say that because this question of feeder lines is one of some importance to anyone considering the establishment of a commercial air line. For instance, I think it is fair to say, although the minister apparently does not like us to say it, that private interests were to a great extent discouraged by government policy wrhen the announcement was made that the railways should divest themselves of their air lines. If that is done to the railways, then who is to know when it will be done to the next private corporation which wishes to operate an air line.
However, the government has stated its policy, and it is that they regard Trans-Canada Air Lines as the agent which will be given exclusive operation rights over main lines. This creates the inference that anyone else, within certain limitations, will be free to start a branch or feeder line. When I say that I do not mean a bush line; I mean a feeder line.
For instance, in my own province, in my own constituency, there might be the desire to establish a line from Vancouver to Calgary,

Trans-Canada Air Lines

which was not served by Trans-Canada Air Lines. That organization provides no service between those two points. A centrally located city, such as Kamloops, might be a stop-over point. There is an airport there capable of accommodating large aircraft.
We are interested in the development of a feeder system throughout central and southern British Columbia, and we foresee that that might be tied in with a north-south line, tying in with the main Trans-Canada Air Line, say at Nelson or some such city.
The point is that nobody is likely to start that sort of undertaking when, all the time, there is hanging over his head the fear that the government may step in and say that that is an area reserved to Trans-Canada Air Lines. That is why I say it is important that the minister should define his policy in respect of feeder and branch lines. Yesterday he said:
Other main lines services are to be added, including for example a service from Winnipeg through Saskatoon to Edmonton.
Without that statement on the record it might be taken by someone, looking at the map, that a line between Edmonton and Winnipeg would be a branch line or a feeder to the main Trans-Canada Air Lines. Therefore he might be prepared to go ahead with that and, after he has his arrangements made, the government comes along suddenly with the statement that that is to be a main line.
I suggest that if the government intends to go ahead with this policy of giving Trans-Canada Air Lines a monopoly control of all main-line operations, then it should lay down immediately a definite policy as to what will be taken to constitute a main line, and, what will constitute a branch or feeder line; because, unless we are to take it that the government policy is one to the effect that there is to be no civil or privately owned commercial organization, then in order to give private individuals the go-ahead sign it must define clearly those areas in which the individual will be free to operate.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
I believe I can relieve my hon. friend's mind. He is afraid that no one, under private enterprise, would wish to tackle the Vancouver-Calgary service. They have made application to the air transport board, and from those applications the board will select the firm best able to give the service.
I think there are many fears in -the minds of hon. members opposite which are not shared by those who are actively at work on air transportation in this country.

speechtext: I must be one of those rare flowers, the night-blooming cereus, as I seem to come out with my estimates late every evening, but I suppose we can carry on with this resolution for the next fifteen or twenty minutes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I wish to refer to one phase of the naval service in which I think a great improvement could be made. The navy is not being demobilized as rapidly as possible, and the pay and allowances for the navy for the present year are almost equal to the expenditure last year and even more than two years ago. This I believe is not because naval personnel cannot be demobilized, nor is it from any lack of shipping, but for some reason best known to the government these men are kept in Nova Scotia', the maritimes and elsewhere, and are not alloived to leave the service as fast as they would like to do. It may be that the election which took place in Nova Scotia to-day had something to do with the matter, and perhaps now the demobilization of naval personnel will proceed a little more rapidly.
I wish to refer particularly to the bandsmen in the navy. They are performing no particularly useful service at the present time and they are very much dissatisfied at being kept in the service. All the other artificers are being kept on in the same manner and it is causing a great deal of dissatisfaction. It means increased cost to the people and it might also interfere with future recruiting. It may be that the minister thinks that by keeping these men in 'the service a certain number of them will join up in the interim period and eventually become members of the permanent navy, but that is not altogether likely to happen, because if they do not join the permanent navy they will go out among the people a bunch of dissatisfied men who will impede rather than help

Demobilization-Naval Services
recruiting for the permanent force. I respect-folly suggest that these men should be allowed to.be discharged and to rehabilitate themselves in private life as they desire to do, because they are serving no useful service at the present moment so far as I can find out. They are not doing any essential work such as the clerks are doing whom it is necessary to retain to assist in the demobilization of the other men. If the government would discharge the bandsmen not oniy would it be in the best interests of the people of Canada and in the best interests of the minister, who is I am sure anxious to recruit the navy up to strength, but it would also be acceding to the wishes of the bandsmen themselves.
Our party has definitely stated its stand on defence. We believe in a strong, efficient army; we believe in a strong, efficient air force; we believe in a strong, efficient navy, and the remarks I have made this evening are made with the pdrpose of helping the government rather than impeding them in their recruiting campaign for the permanent navy.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I am not sure that I caught my hon. friend's question, but I think he complained that we were not demobilizing the navy fast enough. I said yesterday that we were demobilizing at the rate of ten thousand a month, which in my judgment, for what it may be worth, is about as rapidly as we can possibly turn men out without turning them out too quickly. I do not think we should turn them out too fast. The rate of demobilization compares favourably with that of the other services. It is only six or seven weeks since V-J day, and we have already demobilized fifty-three per cent of the total strength of the navy.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I had particular reference to the bandsmen; they are serving no useful purpose at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I am not prepared to concede that bandsmen do not serve a useful purpose in any service. At the outset of the war we had complaints that we did not have enough bands. It was a complaint that I made myself. I thought we wanted a lot of bands to give colour and arouse enthusiasm. I think the navy as well as the other services should have bands. I do not know whether my hon. friend was on Confederation square the other day at the opening of the victory loan campaign when we had an air force band and a navy band from Toronto, and a Royal Mounted Police band, I think, all playing rousing music. I am not prepared to say,
until we are actually down to rock bottom, that we should not have a band in the navy as well as in the other services.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I heartily agree with the minister as to bands when the war and a recruiting campaign are on. I think we made a mistake at the beginning of the war in not having enough bands. A band plays an effective part in arousing enthusiasm, but for some reason or another-it was not the fault of the present minister-the government .decided not to have bands. At the present time, if bands are not necessary for the army,
I do not see how they can be of any service to the navy, because the navy will not be recruited just from the maritimes or other ports where they may now be stationed, but will likely be recruited from all over Canada. So that I cannot see why it is necessary to retain the bandsmen at the present time. The bands that we have in Toronto are gathered together by the different armed forces, and they practice for a certain number of hours each week and receive a certain amount of pay. They do perform as effective work in providing martial music as any band that spends its whole time at that work. If the minister or any of the departments desire a band they can always get a good band from Toronto. The trouble has been that the military bands attached to the reserve forces cannot get work enough to do, and we have made a special effort to have their services used on special occasions when they will receive a certain amount of remuneration to compensate them for the time they have spent in practising.
As I have said. I think these other men who have special qualifications in private life and want to get away should not be held there any longer. I wish the minister would take that into consideration, because I am astonished that pay and allowances of the naval forces have not gone down in the present year to the extent that we should have expected, or to anything like the extent that they have in the other forces.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Pay and allowances are
down- The bandsmen take their turn for demobilization the same as anybody else, and the basic principle in the navy, as in the other services, is that the men with the longest service get out first.
Pay and allowances are down substantially from last year. Last year the estimates were $114,698,835. The estimates for this year are $68,351,247. The actual expenditures last year for pay and allowances were I think, about $123,000,000. I am speaking from memory.

Demobilization-Naval Services
as I have not the figures here. This year they are estimated to be about $98,000,000. So that pay and allowances are down substantially. My hon. friend will recall, if he thinks it over, that on a straight basis of mathematics the average number of men employed during the year will be rather higher than the number who were discharged to date, because you have to include in the figures the thirty days leave granted on discharge, and other items of that kind, so, that in effect a man is on the strength for thirty or forty days after he actually ceases to be a serving rating. The figure for pay and allowances necessarily reflects that amount, but the pay and allowances will not exceed the average number of men on strength during the year. They are being demobilized at the rate of about ten thousand a month; fifty-three per cent have already been demobilized, and by the end of the year we shall be down to the minimum below which we do not want to go.

speechtext:
In the first place I must
congratulate the hon. member for High Park upon his interest in the fine arts and his musical disposition. No doubt upon such a subject the discussion will be carried on in perfect harmony. I am interested in bands- military bands.

speechtext:
Yes; I can give that explanation. One explanation, a very short one, is that the navy operates two industrial establishments in the shape of dockyards on the east and west coast. We have a very large number of civilian employees in those dockyards. Neither the army nor the air force operates any comparable establishment. We still have on the east and west coast large dockyards which employ a very considerable number of civilian employees. As I say, these in effect are industrial establishments. For that reason the ratio of the navy's civilian employees to its service employees is probably higher than in either of the -other services. In addition, we contemplate during the course of this year replacing as many service employees as we can with civilian employees, particularly in clerical work such as is now being carried out by W.-R.C.N.S. and other service personnel.
